stories.title: The Girl Who Caught the Clouds

pages.text: Every morning in the mountains near Abha, the fog rolled into the valley like a slow white tide. Fourteen-year-old Layla liked to watch it from her grandfather's terrace while the rest of the house was still asleep. Below them, the coffee trees on the lower terraces had been struggling for months, because the rains had come late again. "If only we could drink the clouds," her grandfather said, half joking, as he poured the qahwa. Layla didn't laugh, because the idea had already stuck in her mind.

That afternoon she noticed a spider's web glittering between two branches, heavy with tiny drops. Although it hadn't rained for weeks, the web was soaking wet. She crouched down and watched one drop slide along a thread and fall onto a leaf below. Suddenly, everything clicked. The fog wasn't just passing through the valley; it was carrying water that nobody was catching.

The school's annual invention fair was only six weeks away, and Layla had been searching for a project ever since it was announced. Her older brother Omar was sceptical. "A net that catches water from the air? You'll be the laughing stock of the whole school." "People laughed at the first aeroplane too," Layla replied, rolling her eyes. With her mother's permission, she borrowed some fine plastic mesh, two wooden poles and a length of old pipe from the shed.

Her first prototype was simple: the mesh was stretched between the poles, with a pipe underneath leading into a bucket. She set it up on the edge of the terrace before bed, too excited to sleep properly. At dawn she rushed outside, only to find the net ripped and the bucket lying on its side, completely empty. A strong gust in the night had torn the whole thing apart. Omar didn't say a word, but his raised eyebrows said everything.

Layla was tempted to give up, but her grandfather took her for a walk instead. He led her to a crumbling stone wall at the far end of the farm, built long before he was born. "My grandfather told me these walls were built facing a particular direction," he explained, running his hand over the damp stones. "They face the wind, so the fog leaves its water on them, and the water runs down to the roots." Layla stared at the wall in amazement, realising that her ancestors had solved the same problem centuries ago.

Inspired, she redesigned her invention from scratch. This time she angled the net to work with the wind rather than fight it, and she secured the frame with heavy stones, just like the old wall. She also added a second layer of mesh, having read that a double layer traps more drops. Even Omar, who had stopped teasing her, offered to help dig the posts into the ground. The next morning the bucket held almost four litres of clear, cold water, and Layla let out a cry of delight that woke half the house.

By the day of the fair, the improved design had been collecting water every morning for three weeks. Layla presented it alongside photos of the stone wall and a chart showing exactly how much water she had gathered. One of the judges, an engineer from the university, asked her a question she hadn't expected. "Did you invent this, or did you discover it?" Layla hesitated, then answered honestly: "Both, I think. My great-great-grandparents had the idea first; I've just found a new way to use it."

When the results were announced, first prize went to a boy who had built a robot that sorted rubbish. Layla clapped for him sincerely, though she couldn't help feeling a little disappointed. Afterwards, however, the engineer came to find her. "The university is studying ways to bring water to mountain farms," she said. "Would your family let us test a larger version of your nets on your terraces?" Layla was so stunned that, for once in her life, she was lost for words.

By the following spring, a row of tall nets stood along the top of the farm, glittering every morning like enormous spider webs. The coffee trees had turned green again, and two neighbouring farmers had already asked for nets of their own. Layla's grandfather sat on the terrace, pouring the qahwa as usual. "So," he said with a smile, "you really did teach us to drink the clouds." "No, Jiddo," Layla said, looking out at the old stone wall. "We just remembered how."

questions.q: What gave Layla the idea for her invention?
options: A wet spider's web on a dry day
A science programme on television
A robot she saw at school

questions.q: Why did Layla's first prototype fail?
options: The mesh was too thick to catch water
A strong wind destroyed it during the night
Omar moved it while she was asleep

questions.q: In the story, what does "sceptical" mean?
options: Very excited and supportive
Not believing that something will work
Angry and jealous

questions.q: Why did Layla say she both invented and discovered the fog net?
options: She had copied the design from a book
Her ancestors used the same idea, and she found a new way to use it
The engineer had helped her build it

questions.q: What can we infer from Layla's final words to her grandfather?
options: She believes old knowledge was just as important as her invention
She is upset that she didn't win first prize
She thinks the nets will stop working soon

pages.text: Noura had always thought that her grandfather's study smelled of old paper and cardamom. Three months after he passed away, she was helping her father sort through his shelves when a small leather notebook slipped out and landed at her feet. Inside, in faded blue ink, was a diary of a road trip he had taken to Oman in 1978. Tucked between the last two pages was a brass compass, its glass scratched but its needle still trembling towards the north. On the final page, Grandfather had written just one sentence: "One day, I must return this to Salim."

"Who on earth is Salim?" Noura asked, turning the compass over in her hands. Her father shook his head slowly, because he had never heard the name before. They read the diary together that evening, and the story gradually came to life. As a young man, Grandfather had been caught in a sandstorm while driving through the mountains, and his car had broken down near a tiny village. A shepherd called Salim had found him, given him water and dates, and lent him this compass so that he could find his way to the nearest town.

"He kept it for more than forty years," her father murmured. "He must have felt terrible that he never managed to give it back." Noura studied the hand-drawn map inside the cover, with its wobbly lines and the name of a village: Al-Qarn. Before she could stop herself, she said, "Why don't we take it back for him?" To her surprise, her father didn't laugh; instead, he smiled the way Grandfather used to when he was planning something.

Two weeks later, during the school holidays, Noura and her parents set off in the family car with the diary on Noura's lap. She had taken charge of navigation, comparing Grandfather's notes with the map on her phone. The modern highway was smooth and fast, nothing like the rough tracks he had described, and she couldn't help wondering how frightened he must have been. At the border, the officer flicked through their passports and asked about the purpose of their visit. "We're returning something that was borrowed," Noura replied, and the officer raised his eyebrows with a puzzled smile.

Finding the village turned out to be far harder than they had expected. Al-Qarn didn't appear on any online map, and the first three people they asked had never heard of it. By the second afternoon, as the car climbed narrow roads between steep, rust-coloured cliffs, Noura was beginning to feel they were looking for a needle in a haystack. Then she noticed a lonely fig tree beside a dry riverbed, exactly like the one sketched in the diary. "Stop the car!" she shouted. "Grandfather drew this tree!"

Beyond the tree, a dusty path led to a cluster of stone houses clinging to the mountainside. An elderly man in a white dishdasha was sitting outside a small shop, and he watched them curiously as they approached. Noura's father greeted him politely and explained, a little nervously, why they had come. The man listened in silence, but when Noura held out the compass, his eyes widened. "That belonged to my father," he said quietly. "My name is Hamad, and I am Salim's son."

Hamad invited them into his home, where his wife served coffee in tiny cups along with a plate of sweet dates. He explained that Salim had passed away ten years earlier, but he had often told the story of the young Saudi traveller lost in the storm. "My father always said the man would come back one day," Hamad said, shaking his head in wonder. "We used to tease him about it, because we thought the stranger had simply forgotten." Noura felt a lump in her throat as she realised that both old men had remembered each other for a lifetime.

When Noura placed the compass in Hamad's hands, he turned it over gently, just as she had done in Grandfather's study. Then, to everyone's surprise, he pushed it back towards her. "My father lent it so that a traveller could find his way," he said. "Now it has guided you all the way here, so it belongs with someone who still has many journeys ahead of her." Noura tried to refuse, but Hamad insisted, and her father gave her a small nod to show that she should accept.

Before they left, Hamad's family made them promise to visit again, and Noura wrote their address carefully inside the diary. On the long drive home, she held the compass up to the window and watched the needle settle steadily towards the north. She realised that the trip had never really been about returning an object; it had been about finishing a story that Grandfather had started. Now, she thought, the next chapter was hers to write. Under Grandfather's final sentence, she added one line of her own: "Returned, and given back again."

questions.q: Where did Noura first find the compass?
options: Between the last two pages of her grandfather's diary
In a drawer in her grandfather's car
In a small shop in Oman

questions.q: In Page 5, what does "looking for a needle in a haystack" mean?
options: Doing hard work on a farm
Searching for something that is almost impossible to find
Looking for something sharp and dangerous

questions.q: How did Noura recognise that they were close to the village?
options: An officer at the border gave them directions
Hamad was waiting for them by the road
She saw a fig tree that matched a drawing in the diary

questions.q: Why did Hamad give the compass back to Noura?
options: He believed it should keep helping a traveller with journeys ahead
He thought it was broken and no longer useful
He did not believe it had belonged to his father

questions.q: What does Noura's final line in the diary suggest?
options: She was disappointed that the trip had failed
The story of the compass is continuing with her
She plans to sell the compass one day

pages.text: Faisal Al-Harbi had always loved football, but at fifteen he had discovered something he loved even more: refereeing. While his friends dreamed of scoring goals, he studied the rules until he knew them by heart. Every Friday after prayers, he watched matches with a notebook and wrote down every decision he would have made differently. His father found it strange at first, but eventually he bought Faisal a proper black whistle. "If you're going to do this," he said, "do it properly."

After months of training courses in Riyadh, Faisal was chosen to referee the final of the city's under-16 tournament. It was an enormous honour, especially for someone so young. However, when he saw the team list, his heart sank. The captain of Al-Nakheel Academy was his cousin Majed, who had practically grown up in the same house as him. Faisal wondered whether he should ask to be replaced, but his coach, Ustadh Saleh, told him that a good referee never runs away from a difficult situation.

On the night of the final, the stadium was packed with families waving scarves and flags. Faisal's grandmother was sitting in the front row, and he could tell from her proud smile that she expected great things from both of her grandsons. During the warm-up, Majed jogged past and winked at him. "Don't forget who taught you to ride a bike," he joked. Faisal laughed, but the comment stayed in his mind like a stone in his shoe.

The first half was fast and fierce, and Faisal had to keep his cool as players argued over every throw-in. He showed two yellow cards, one to each side, so nobody could accuse him of being unfair. At half-time the score was 1–1, and the crowd was getting louder by the minute. In the changing room, Faisal splashed cold water on his face and reminded himself of his father's words. Tonight he was not anyone's cousin; he was the referee.

With three minutes left and the score still level, Al-Waha's striker broke through the defence. Majed raced back and threw himself into a desperate tackle inside the penalty area. The striker fell, and thousands of people jumped to their feet at once. Faisal had been perfectly positioned, and he had seen it clearly: Majed had caught the player's ankle, not the ball. For a second, the noise seemed to disappear, and he could hear only his own heartbeat.

Faisal blew his whistle and pointed firmly to the penalty spot. The Al-Nakheel players surrounded him, shouting that he had made a terrible mistake. Majed stared at him in disbelief, his face red with anger. "Are you serious?" he demanded. "You know I'd never tackle like that!" Faisal said nothing; he simply showed him a yellow card and calmly asked the players to step back.

The striker scored, and Al-Waha won the cup. As the winners celebrated, Faisal walked off the pitch without looking at the stands, convinced that half the stadium hated him. He hardly slept that night, replaying the moment in his head again and again. By the next morning, he was dreading the family lunch at his grandmother's house, where Majed would certainly be waiting.

When Faisal arrived, his cousin was sitting in the majlis with his phone in his hand. Without a word, Majed showed him a video filmed from the stands and slowed down frame by frame. It proved that his boot had struck the striker's ankle. "I've watched it twenty times," Majed admitted, looking embarrassed. "I was wrong to shout at you. If you had let it go, I'd always have known the cup wasn't really ours."

A week later, a letter arrived from the regional football association. Faisal had been selected for the national youth refereeing programme, partly because an observer had praised his "courage and calm under pressure" in the final. At lunch, his grandmother asked Majed what he thought of the news. Majed grinned and put an arm around his cousin's shoulders. "He's the toughest referee I've ever played against," he said, "and the fairest."

questions.q: Why did Faisal consider asking to be replaced as referee of the final?
options: His cousin was the captain of one of the teams.
He felt he was too young and inexperienced.
His coach did not think he was ready.

questions.q: What does the phrase "keep his cool" mean in the story?
options: Stay out of the hot sun
Remain calm and in control
Avoid making any decisions

questions.q: Why did Faisal give Al-Waha a penalty near the end of the match?
options: Majed had touched the ball with his hand.
The striker had pretended to fall.
Majed had kicked the striker's ankle instead of the ball.

questions.q: What does Majed's comment "the cup wasn't really ours" suggest about him?
options: He did not care about winning the tournament.
He values winning fairly more than just winning.
He thought Al-Waha were the better team all season.

questions.q: Why was Faisal selected for the national youth refereeing programme?
options: His grandmother wrote to the football association.
An observer praised how he handled pressure in the final.
Majed recommended him to the association.

stories.title: The Iron Road and the Old Guide

pages.text: In the summer of 1908, the whole city of Madinah was talking about one thing: the iron road. For years, workers had been laying tracks across the desert from Damascus, and now the Hejaz Railway was almost complete. Fourteen-year-old Hamza could hardly sleep at night, imagining the great black engine rolling into the new station. His grandfather, Saleh, however, was far from impressed. "I have guided caravans through this desert for forty years," he grumbled. "No smoking monster will ever understand the sand the way a camel does."

Hamza had been running errands at the station for months, and the station master, Mr. Kamal, had taken a liking to him. He had even shown Hamza how the telegraph worked, tapping messages along the wire that followed the tracks. "Messages travel faster than any rider," Mr. Kamal explained, "as long as the line stays up." That evening, Hamza tried to share his excitement at dinner, but his grandfather simply shook his head. "Machines are clever," the old man said, "but the desert is cleverer."

A week before the grand opening, Saleh had to collect dates from a village to the north, and he asked Hamza to come along. They set off before dawn on two of the family's camels, following an ancient route that ran close to the new railway. Around midday, his grandfather suddenly stopped and stared at the horizon. The sky had turned a strange yellow colour, and the air felt heavy and still. "Get down," he ordered calmly. "A storm is coming, and it won't wait for us."

They led the camels behind a group of large rocks and made them kneel, then wrapped their scarves tightly around their faces. Within minutes, the wind was howling and the sun had completely disappeared. Hamza pressed himself against the warm side of his camel, his heart pounding. Through the roar, he could hear his grandfather reciting verses from the Quran in a steady voice, and gradually his fear began to fade. The storm raged for nearly three hours before it finally blew itself out.

When they climbed out, the landscape looked completely different. Hamza ran to the top of a small hill and gasped. Below them, in a narrow cutting between two ridges, the railway had vanished under a huge new dune. Worse still, the telegraph pole beside it had been knocked flat, and its wire lay buried in the sand. "The afternoon train from the north is due to pass here before sunset," Hamza whispered. "If the driver doesn't see the sand in time, the whole train could come off the rails."

For a moment, neither of them spoke, and Hamza realised that no message could warn anyone now. Then his grandfather placed a firm hand on his shoulder. "My knees are too old for a fast ride, but yours are not," he said. "Follow the tracks north, but cut across the dry valley where the line bends, and you will save an hour." He pulled off his red headscarf and pressed it into Hamza's hands. "Wave this as if your life depends on it, because other lives certainly do."

Hamza rode harder than he had ever ridden before, his camel's long legs eating up the ground. By the time he crossed the valley, the sun was sinking fast and his throat was burning with thirst. Then he saw it: a thin column of black smoke rising in the distance. He drove his camel up onto the tracks, stood up in the saddle and waved the red scarf wildly above his head. With a terrible screech of metal, the engine slowed, and finally came to a stop only a few metres in front of him.

The driver jumped down, red-faced and furious, but his anger disappeared once Hamza had explained what lay ahead. Soon, passengers and crew were walking south together, carrying every shovel the train had on board. When they reached the cutting, they found Saleh already there with a dozen men from the nearby village, who had seen the storm and come to help. Working side by side under the rising moon, they cleared the track before midnight. The driver shook the old man's hand warmly. "You and your grandson saved us all tonight," he said.

On the first of September, when the railway was officially opened, Mr. Kamal called Hamza and his grandfather to the front of the crowd to thank them in front of everyone. Hamza noticed that his grandfather was watching the shining engine with a new kind of respect. "Perhaps this monster is not so bad," Saleh admitted with a smile, "but it still needs a camel now and then." Years later, Hamza became one of the first engineers from Madinah to work on the line. Whenever young workers asked him for advice, he always gave the same answer: "Trust your machines, but never stop listening to the desert."

questions.q: What did Mr. Kamal teach Hamza at the station?
options: How to drive the engine
How the telegraph worked
How to repair the tracks

questions.q: Why could Hamza and his grandfather not send a message to warn the train?
options: The telegraph wire had been knocked down and buried
Mr. Kamal was not at the station
They did not know how to use the telegraph

questions.q: In the story, the word "vanished" is closest in meaning to:
options: broke
disappeared
moved

questions.q: Why did Saleh send Hamza instead of going himself?
options: He was afraid of the train
He wanted to stay with the dates
He was too old to ride fast

questions.q: What does Saleh's comment at the opening suggest about how his opinion had changed?
options: He now hated the railway even more
He had started to respect the railway but still valued traditional knowledge
He wanted to sell all his camels

pages.text: Every Eid, the whole family gathered at Grandma Noura's house in Taif, and every Eid, her chicken kabsa was the star of the meal. This year, however, Grandma had flown to Riyadh to visit Aunt Huda, and she was supposed to be back by noon. At ten o'clock, Faisal's phone buzzed with a message that made his stomach drop: "Flight delayed. Start the kabsa without me. The notebook is in the top drawer." Faisal was fourteen and had never cooked anything more complicated than an omelette. He stared at the screen in disbelief.

His sister Lama, who was sixteen and considered herself the sensible one, found the notebook within seconds. It was a battered old thing with a cracked leather cover, and its yellowed pages were covered in Grandma's curly handwriting. They quickly turned to the page marked "Kabsa for thirty," and Lama groaned. At some point, someone had spilled a whole cup of tea across it, and half of the ingredients had faded into a brown blur. "We can read 'rice', 'chicken' and 'onions'," she said, "but the spices have completely disappeared."

Faisal tried calling Grandma, but the call went straight to voicemail, which meant her phone had either died or been switched off for the flight. Thirty guests were expected at two o'clock, and the kitchen suddenly felt enormous and unfriendly. "We could just order from a restaurant," Faisal suggested, though he already knew what Lama would say. "And tell Grandma her Eid kabsa was replaced by a takeaway? Not a chance." She tied her hair back, washed her hands and handed him an apron.

They began with what they could read: the onions, which Faisal chopped with streaming eyes, and the chicken, which Lama browned in Grandma's huge pot. When it came to the spices, though, they hit a wall. The spice cupboard held at least twenty jars, many of them unlabelled, and both of them were reluctant to guess. Then Faisal had an idea. "Close your eyes," he said, "and try to remember what the kitchen smells like when Grandma is cooking."

Feeling slightly ridiculous, Lama did as he said, and after a moment a faint smile crossed her face. "Cardamom," she said slowly, "definitely cardamom, and something warm, like cinnamon." Faisal opened jar after jar, sniffing each one carefully, until he found a small dark one that made him laugh out loud. Inside were dried black limes, the bitter, smoky loomi that Grandma always dropped into the pot whole. "I'd recognise that smell anywhere," he said. "It's the smell of every Eid I can remember."

By midday, the pot was bubbling away and the kitchen smelled almost, but not quite, right. Something was missing, and neither of them could work out what it was. They argued about adding more salt, then about cumin, until Lama threw up her hands and declared that too many cooks spoil the broth. "There are only two of us," Faisal pointed out, and they both burst out laughing despite their nerves. Then he remembered something: before every big meal, Grandma heated a dry pan, and the house filled with a sweet, nutty smell.

"She toasts the whole spices first!" Lama cried. "That's what we've forgotten!" They toasted cardamom pods, cloves and coriander seeds until the smell flooded the room, and this time they both knew immediately that it was right. At two o'clock sharp, the doorbell began to ring, and uncles, aunts and cousins poured into the house. Faisal and Lama carried out large platters of golden rice and chicken, topped with fried almonds, trying to look far calmer than they felt. There was still no sign of Grandma.

Just as everyone was sitting down, the front door opened and Grandma walked in, tired but smiling, having arrived in the nick of time. She sat down without a word, took a spoonful of kabsa and chewed thoughtfully while the whole room fell silent. "This isn't my kabsa," she said at last, and Faisal's heart sank. Then her eyes began to shine. "It's yours," she continued, "and I'm almost sorry to say it's very nearly better than mine."

Later, Faisal showed her the ruined page and apologised for the tea stain. To his surprise, Grandma laughed. "That page was never much use, habibi. I stopped measuring things forty years ago, and I cook with my nose and my memory, exactly as you two did today." She took a pen, turned to a fresh page and wrote in her curly handwriting: "Kabsa by Faisal and Lama, to be cooked again next Eid." Faisal smiled, realising that the most important ingredients had never been written in any notebook at all.

questions.q: Why did Faisal and Lama have to cook the kabsa themselves?
options: Grandma's flight was delayed
Grandma was ill in bed
The restaurant was closed for Eid

questions.q: What had happened to the recipe page in the notebook?
options: It had been torn out
Tea had been spilled on it
It was written in a language they could not read

questions.q: In the text, the word "reluctant" (page 4) is closest in meaning to:
options: excited
unwilling
able

questions.q: How did the brother and sister finally discover the missing step?
options: They searched for a recipe online
An aunt explained it to them
Faisal remembered a smell from Grandma's cooking

questions.q: What does Grandma's final message suggest about cooking?
options: Good cooking depends on memory and experience, not only written recipes
Recipes should always be followed exactly
Young people should not cook for large groups

pages.text: Yousef had always believed that superheroes belonged in comic books, not in Jeddah. Then, one Thursday evening, while he was clearing out his grandfather's dusty storeroom, he came across an old brass compass whose needle didn't point north. It pointed straight at him. The moment he picked it up, the whole city fell silent: the car horns, the seagulls, even the ceiling fan stopped mid-turn. Exactly sixty seconds later, everything burst back into motion as if nothing had happened.

Over the weekend, Yousef tested the compass as carefully as a scientist. He discovered that it worked only once a day, that the freeze always lasted sixty seconds, and that nobody else ever noticed a thing. By Saturday night, he had caught his brother's falling phone, saved a plate of kunafa from crashing to the floor, and won a game of chess by secretly moving his opponent's queen, which he wasn't exactly proud of. "I'm basically a superhero," he whispered to his reflection. "All I need is a name." His reflection, unfortunately, didn't look convinced.

On Sunday morning, Yousef sat down to a maths test he had barely revised for. His classmate Faisal's paper was lying open on the next desk, every answer clearly visible. His fingers closed around the compass in his pocket, and he realised he could copy the whole page in the blink of an eye. Then he remembered something his grandfather often said: "A man is what he does when no one is watching." Yousef let go of the compass, did his best, and got seventy-one percent, yet he walked out of the classroom feeling strangely lighter.

That evening, his grandfather, whom everyone called Jiddo, noticed the compass on Yousef's desk, and his face went pale. "Where did you find that?" he asked quietly. Yousef was sure he was about to be told off for going through the storeroom without permission. Instead, Jiddo sat down slowly on the edge of the bed and sighed. "So it has chosen you too," he said.

Jiddo explained that the compass had found him when he was seventeen, back in the days when the old souq was still full of wooden shops. One afternoon, a fire broke out, so he froze time and raced inside to help a shopkeeper who was trapped behind a fallen shelf. However, sixty seconds turned out to be far too short, and he simply didn't know how to move an injured man safely. Luckily, the firefighters arrived just in time, but it had been a very close call. "That day I learned that sixty seconds is almost nothing if you don't know what to do with them," Jiddo said, "so I became a paramedic and never used the compass again."

"So using it is wrong?" Yousef asked, feeling rather confused. "Not wrong," Jiddo replied, "just not enough. Being a hero isn't about stopping time; it's about being ready when time doesn't stop." Yousef kept thinking about those words all week, although he wasn't completely sure what they meant. The following Friday, the whole family gathered for a picnic on the Corniche, and the sea breeze carried the smell of grilled corn and cardamom coffee.

Suddenly, an elderly man at the next table clutched his chest and collapsed onto the grass. Without hesitating, Yousef grabbed the compass, and the world froze around him. He sprinted over to the man, knelt beside him, and then the penny dropped: he had absolutely no idea how to help. The seconds were ticking away, and all his amazing power had given him was time to panic. With only a few seconds left, he ran back and stood right beside Jiddo, ready to shout the instant the world started again.

"Jiddo, that man!" Yousef yelled as the sounds of the Corniche came rushing back. His grandfather was on his feet immediately and began giving the man CPR, calm and steady, while he told Yousef to call 997. By the time the ambulance arrived, the man was breathing again, and one of the paramedics said the first few minutes had probably saved his life. Yousef understood then that it hadn't been his frozen sixty seconds that made the difference. It had been an old man's hands that knew exactly what to do.

The next morning, Yousef signed up for a first aid course with the Saudi Red Crescent, and he persuaded Faisal to join him too. He placed the compass carefully in his drawer, deciding that he would only use it once he had learned enough to make those sixty seconds count. "So, have you chosen your superhero name yet?" Jiddo asked with a smile. "Not yet," Yousef replied, "but I know what my first real power is going to be." When he glanced into the drawer, he noticed that, for the very first time, the needle was pointing north.

questions.q: What did Yousef do with the compass during the maths test?
options: He used it to copy Faisal's answers
He let go of it and did the test honestly
He gave it to his teacher

questions.q: Why did Jiddo stop using the compass when he was young?
options: He realised that time alone was useless without the right skills
The compass stopped working after the fire
His parents took it away from him

questions.q: In the story, what does "the penny dropped" mean?
options: Yousef lost some money on the grass
Yousef suddenly understood something
Yousef dropped the compass

questions.q: Who actually saved the elderly man's life?
options: Yousef, by freezing time
Faisal, by calling the ambulance
Jiddo, by giving him CPR

questions.q: What does the needle pointing north at the end most likely suggest?
options: The compass is finally broken
Yousef has found the right direction for his life
Jiddo has secretly fixed the compass

stories.title: The Ghost of the Lost Property Box

pages.text: Yousef had been the editor of the school newspaper, The Al-Noor Voice, for exactly three weeks, and he was already running out of ideas. The deadline for the next issue was Thursday, and so far he had nothing more exciting than a report on the new water fountains. "Nobody is going to read this," he groaned, staring at his empty screen in the newspaper office. At that moment, his best friend Hamad burst through the door, waving a calculator in one hand and a folded piece of paper in the other. "It's happened again!" Hamad announced breathlessly.

Hamad had lost his calculator two days earlier, and that morning he had found it waiting for him in the lost property box, with a note attached. The handwriting was neat and slightly old-fashioned, written in dark blue ink: "Found under the bench near the science lab. Good luck in your maths test, and remember to check your minus signs." It was the third note like this that month, and the boys had started calling the mysterious writer "the Ghost." Nobody had ever seen the Ghost, yet the Ghost seemed to know everyone's worries. Yousef sat up straight, suddenly wide awake, because he knew he had just found his story.

For the next two days, Yousef and Hamad investigated like real detectives. They collected every note they could find and noticed that each one had appeared before the first bell, when the school was almost empty. Their main suspect was Mr. Adel, the Arabic teacher, who was famous for his beautiful handwriting and his habit of arriving early. However, Hamad soon discovered that Mr. Adel had been away at a conference in Riyadh last week, when two of the notes had appeared. "We've hit a dead end," Hamad sighed, dropping his head onto the desk. Yousef refused to give up, though, and he came up with a plan that was bold, if a little uncomfortable.

At a quarter past six the next morning, while the sky above Jeddah was still pale and grey, the two boys were hiding behind a pillar near the lost property box. The corridors were so silent that Yousef could hear the hum of the air conditioning. Twenty minutes passed, and Hamad, who had not had breakfast, was beginning to complain under his breath. Then they heard it: slow footsteps, accompanied by the soft squeak of wheels. A figure appeared at the end of the corridor, pushing a mop bucket, with a small blue pen tucked behind his ear.

It was Uncle Saleh, the school caretaker, who had been looking after the building for nearly thirty years. The boys watched in amazement as he took a pencil case out of his pocket, wrote a few lines on a scrap of paper, and placed both carefully in the box. When Yousef stepped out from behind the pillar, Uncle Saleh jumped, almost knocking over his bucket. For a moment he looked embarrassed, but then his face broke into a warm, tired smile. "So," he said quietly, "the newspaper has caught the Ghost at last."

Sitting on a bench in the empty courtyard, Uncle Saleh explained everything. He had left school at the age of twelve to support his family, and he had always regretted not finishing his education. For the past two years, he had been studying every night for his secondary school certificate, and his final exams were only two weeks away. "I hear the boys talking about their tests while I clean the corridors," he admitted, "and writing those notes helps me practise and remember what I've learned." Then his voice became serious as he asked them to keep his secret under wraps, because if he failed, he did not want the whole school to know.

That evening, Yousef faced the hardest decision of his short career as an editor. Hamad kept reminding him that this was the biggest scoop the school newspaper had ever had, and that everyone was desperate to know who the Ghost was. Yousef knew Hamad was right, but he also remembered the worried look in Uncle Saleh's eyes. In the end, he wrote an article called "Some Mysteries Deserve to Stay Mysteries," describing the kindness of the notes without revealing who had written them. To his surprise, it became the most popular article the newspaper had published all year.

A month later, Uncle Saleh came to the newspaper office holding an envelope, and his hands were trembling slightly. He had passed every single exam, and he told Yousef that he could finally write the full story. The following Sunday, the principal read Yousef's article aloud in the morning assembly, and when he announced the Ghost's real identity, the courtyard fell completely silent. Then, one by one, hundreds of students and teachers rose to their feet and applauded until their hands hurt. Uncle Saleh, standing at the back with his mop, had tears in his eyes as the principal presented him with a certificate in front of the whole school.

The next morning, Yousef arrived early, out of habit, and glanced at the lost property box as he passed. Inside, there was a folded note with his own name written on it in familiar dark blue ink. "Dear Editor," it said, "anyone can rush to tell a story, but it takes real wisdom to know when to wait. Your patience gave me the courage to finish what I started forty years ago." Yousef smiled and put the note carefully in his pocket, where he would keep it for many years. He had learned that the best stories are not always the fastest ones, but the ones told with respect.

stories.title: The Key Under the Fig Tree

pages.text: Nobody in the Al-Harbi family ever mentioned Uncle Saad. Whenever his name came up, Grandpa Abdullah would suddenly become very interested in his coffee, and the room would fall silent. Fifteen-year-old Yousef had grown used to it, the way you get used to a door that is always locked. But that changed one Thursday evening in Jeddah, when he was helping his grandfather clear out the storeroom. Behind a pile of old carpets, he found a rusty tin with a tiny brass key taped to the lid.

Inside the tin was a folded piece of paper, yellow with age. It was a hand-drawn map of a farm, with a well, a row of palm trees and a large fig tree marked with a careful X. Underneath, someone had written in shaky Arabic: "For my two sons, when they are ready." Yousef's older sister, Reem, leaned over his shoulder and gasped. "That's Great-grandfather's handwriting," she whispered. "I've seen it in the old notebook upstairs."

When they showed Grandpa the map, his face turned pale. For a long moment he said nothing, and Yousef was afraid they had made a terrible mistake. Finally, the old man sighed. "That is our father's farm near Taif," he said quietly. "My brother Saad and I argued about it after he passed away, and we both said things we should never have said. We haven't spoken for twenty-two years." Reem and Yousef exchanged a glance, because at last the locked door had opened a crack.

That night, Yousef couldn't sleep. If their great-grandfather had hidden something for both his sons, surely it was meant to bring them together, not to keep them apart. The next morning, he and Reem persuaded their father to drive them up the mountain road to Taif. "Your grandfather won't like this," Baba warned, but there was a hint of curiosity in his eyes. Three hours later, they were standing in front of a crumbling mud wall, and the cool mountain air smelled of roses.

The farm had been empty for years, and weeds had taken over almost everything. Still, the old well was exactly where the map showed it, and beyond it stood an enormous fig tree, its branches heavy with fruit. Just as Yousef started digging at its roots, a pickup truck rattled up the track and stopped in a cloud of dust. A tall, grey-bearded man climbed out, frowning. "This is private land!" he called. "Who are you, and what are you doing to my father's tree?"

Baba stepped forward and greeted him politely. "Uncle Saad?" he said slowly. "I'm Khalid, Abdullah's son, and these are my children." The man froze, and for a second Yousef thought he might get back in his truck and drive away. Instead, his frown softened, and he looked at Reem and Yousef as though he were seeing ghosts. "You have your grandfather's eyes," he told Yousef, his voice rough. "He was about your age when we used to climb this tree together."

Yousef held out the map, and Uncle Saad read the shaky words twice before he spoke. "So it really existed," he murmured. "Our father always told us there was a 'treasure' here, but we thought it was just a story." Together they kept digging, and soon Yousef's shovel struck something hard. It was a small metal box, and the brass key from the tin fitted the lock perfectly. Inside, wrapped in cloth, lay two letters, one for each brother, and a faded photograph of two little boys laughing under the fig tree.

Uncle Saad's letter was short. "A farm can be divided," their great-grandfather had written, "but a family cannot be divided without breaking. Look after each other first, and the land second." The old man turned away and wiped his eyes with the end of his shemagh. "We wasted so many years arguing about a few palm trees, when this was what he wanted all along," he said. Reem gently handed him the second letter. "Then maybe you should deliver this one yourself," she suggested.

The following Friday, after the prayer, a pickup truck pulled up outside Grandpa's house in Jeddah. Yousef opened the door, and the two old brothers stood facing each other in silence, neither of them knowing how to break the ice. Then Uncle Saad held out the letter and the photograph, and Grandpa's hands began to shake. A moment later they were embracing like the boys in the picture, and the whole family crowded into the majlis, where Mama poured coffee and served dates and fresh figs from Taif. From that day on, nobody in the Al-Harbi family ever fell silent at the mention of Uncle Saad again.

pages.text: Layan Al-Ghamdi had always believed that the most interesting technology was the kind nobody noticed. While her classmates in Abha talked about the newest phones, she spent her evenings in the corner of her father's garage, surrounded by wires, batteries and a small soldering iron. Her grandfather, who lived in a village in the mountains, called the corner "the laboratory", half joking and half proud. That spring, her school announced a regional innovation competition with one simple rule: solve a real problem in your community. Layan knew immediately what hers would be.

Every few years, heavy rain turned the dry valley below her grandfather's village into a rushing river within minutes. People called these sudden floods "the wadi waking up", and the wadi rarely gave a warning. Two winters earlier, a neighbour's pickup truck had been swept off the road, and although the driver had escaped, the memory still frightened everyone. "If only the water could tell us it was coming," her grandfather had said once, looking down at the empty riverbed. Layan had never forgotten those words.

Her plan was to build a small device that would sit on a rock upstream, measure the water level and send an alert to the village the moment it started rising. She would power it with a solar panel, because there was no electricity in the valley, and protect it with a waterproof box. Her older brother Faisal, who was studying engineering at university, agreed to help with the programming at weekends. "It's ambitious," he warned her, "but ambitious is better than boring." For six weeks, they worked against the clock, testing the sensor in a bucket of water on the garage floor.

The night before the competition, everything that could go wrong did. The signal that had worked perfectly in the garage kept disappearing, and the messages arrived late or not at all. At midnight, Faisal discovered the problem: the mountains blocked the mobile network, so the device needed to send its alert by radio to a receiver in the village first. "So we're back to square one," Layan said, staring at the screen. "Not square one," Faisal replied, rubbing his tired eyes. "Maybe square three."

At the competition, the judges walked past tables covered with shiny robots and colourful apps. When they reached Layan's table, they found a plain grey box, a solar panel and a notebook full of crossed-out calculations. She explained the radio problem honestly and admitted that the device had never been tested in a real flood. One judge nodded politely, but another frowned and said, "An idea is only as good as the evidence behind it." Layan's project did not win a prize, and she rode home with her family in silence.

That evening, her grandfather phoned. "Bring your grey box anyway," he said. "The wadi is a better judge than any committee." The following weekend, the whole family drove up to the village, and Faisal and Layan fixed the device to a large rock two kilometres upstream. They placed the receiver on her grandfather's roof, connected to a loud alarm and a red light. Then there was nothing to do but wait for clouds that might not come for months.

The clouds came three weeks later, on a Thursday night when Layan was staying at her grandfather's house. The rain began gently, tapping on the windows, and then suddenly it was pouring so hard that she could barely hear her own voice. At 10:47, the red light on the roof began to flash and the alarm filled the house. Her grandfather was already reaching for his phone. "The water is rising upstream," he told the neighbours, one after another. "Nobody use the valley road tonight."

Twenty minutes later, a wall of brown water thundered down the wadi, exactly where the road crossed the valley. From the roof, by the light of their torches, they watched it carry rocks and branches away as if they weighed nothing. Down the hill, Abu Saleh, a farmer who usually drove home late from the market, had turned back after receiving the call. In the morning, he came to the house with a basket of fresh dates and shook Layan's hand warmly. "Your grey box," he said quietly, "is worth more than any shiny robot."

News travels fast in small villages, and soon the regional council asked Layan and Faisal to install sensors in three more valleys. The judge who had frowned at the competition wrote to her school to request a meeting, and this time he wanted to hear every detail. Layan realised that her favourite kind of technology had not changed: it was still the kind that nobody noticed, until the moment it mattered most. Back in the garage, she opened a new notebook and began to sketch her next design. Her grandfather's wish had come true after all: the water could tell them it was coming. All they had needed was a way to listen.

stories.title: The Madman Who Caught the Light

pages.text: In the spring of 1011, the streets of Cairo were full of rumours about the madman who lived near the great mosque of al-Azhar. People said he had once been the cleverest scholar in Egypt, but now he talked to walls and laughed at nothing. Fourteen-year-old Yusuf had never believed half of what he heard in the market, yet his hands were shaking when the guards opened the heavy wooden door. His uncle, who usually delivered the man's bread and lentils, had fallen ill, so the job had suddenly become Yusuf's. "Leave the food and get out quickly," one guard muttered. "And whatever he says, don't take it seriously."

The room was surprisingly tidy, with piles of paper stacked neatly against every wall. A thin man with a grey beard was sitting by the window, and he looked up with eyes that seemed anything but mad. "Close the shutters, would you?" he asked politely, as if Yusuf were a guest rather than a delivery boy. When Yusuf did so, the room went dark except for a single beam of light coming through a tiny hole in the wood. On the opposite wall, faint but unmistakable, appeared the street outside: a camel, a fruit seller and a boy running past, all of them upside down.

Yusuf nearly dropped the basket. "Is this magic?" he whispered, staring at the moving picture on the wall. "Not at all," the man replied with a smile. "It is simply light, and light always tells the truth if you are patient enough to listen." Then he lowered his voice and added, "My name is al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham, and I am no more mad than you are." Yusuf wondered whether that was exactly what a madman would say, but something in the scholar's calm voice made him stay.

Over the following weeks, as Yusuf brought the food each morning, Ibn al-Haytham slowly told him his story. Years earlier, he had boasted that he could build a dam to control the floods of the Nile, and the powerful Caliph al-Hakim had summoned him to Egypt to do it. "I had bitten off far more than I could chew," he admitted. When he travelled south to Aswan and saw how wide and wild the river was, he realised his plan could never work. Everyone knew that the caliph had a fierce temper and did not forgive failure easily. "So I made a difficult choice," the scholar said quietly. "I pretended to lose my mind, and they locked me in this house instead of punishing me."

"But you could have spent all these years doing nothing," Yusuf said. Ibn al-Haytham shook his head firmly. "A prison is only a prison if you stop thinking," he replied. He explained that for centuries, great Greek thinkers had claimed that our eyes send out rays to touch the things we see. Through his experiments in the dark room, he had proved the opposite: light travels in straight lines from objects into our eyes. "Never trust an idea just because a famous person wrote it," he told Yusuf. "Test it, and let the evidence decide."

Soon Yusuf was not merely delivering bread but helping with experiments. One afternoon, the scholar asked him to place three candles in a row outside the hole, each at a slightly different height. On the wall, three small spots of light appeared, but in reverse order, the highest candle making the lowest spot. When Yusuf covered one candle with his hand, only its spot disappeared. "You see?" Ibn al-Haytham exclaimed, his eyes shining. "Each beam travels on its own path without mixing with the others, and now you have seen it with your own eyes."

Their excitement almost cost them everything. One day, the older guard heard laughter and burst into the room just as Yusuf was writing down measurements. For a terrible moment, Yusuf was sure the secret was out. Thinking quickly, he held up the paper and sighed loudly. "He made me draw his dreams again," he complained, rolling his eyes. "Last week it was flying fish, and today it's candles that talk." The guard laughed, shook his head and left, while Yusuf and the scholar struggled to keep a straight face.

In 1021, extraordinary news spread through Cairo: Caliph al-Hakim had ridden out into the hills one night and had never returned. Within days, the danger that had hung over Ibn al-Haytham for a decade had vanished. Yusuf, now twenty and taller than the scholar himself, was standing beside him when the door was finally opened. Ibn al-Haytham stepped into the sunlight, closed his eyes and breathed deeply. "Ten years," he said softly. "I lost my freedom, but I found something far greater than the dam I once promised."

Many years later, Yusuf stood in front of a class of young students, holding a thick handwritten volume called the Book of Optics. Its pages had already been copied and carried to libraries across the Muslim world, and one day they would travel to Europe and inspire scientists for centuries. "The man who wrote this was called mad," Yusuf told the curious faces in front of him. "In fact, he was the most sensible person I have ever met." Then he closed the shutters, made a tiny hole in the wood and smiled as the world outside appeared, upside down, on the classroom wall.

pages.text: Faisal had built the weather station himself the summer he turned fourteen, using a kit his uncle had sent from Riyadh and a great deal of patience. Now it stood on the flat roof of his family's house in a small town near Taif: a white box of sensors measuring temperature, humidity, wind speed and air pressure. Every evening, he uploaded the readings to his laptop and compared them with the official forecasts. His younger sister Noura teased him constantly, calling him "the Weatherman," but secretly she enjoyed checking the numbers with him. Their grandfather, however, was less impressed. "In my day, we read the sky, not a screen," he would say, tapping his walking stick on the floor.

That Thursday, the whole family was buzzing with excitement. The cousins were coming from Jeddah, and Grandfather had decided that they would all spend Friday in the wadi, a wide, dry valley about twenty minutes from town. The aunts were already preparing rice and grilled chicken, and the younger children had been promised a fire and tea under the acacia trees. The sky was a perfect, cloudless blue, and the forecast predicted sunshine all weekend. Nobody imagined that anything could spoil their plans.

Late that night, Faisal noticed something strange. The air pressure on his screen had been falling steadily for six hours, and the humidity had risen sharply. When he checked the satellite maps online, he saw a cluster of storm clouds forming over the mountains to the east, far beyond the horizon. "Noura, come and look at this," he whispered. "If it rains heavily up there, all that water will run downhill, straight into the wadi." Noura frowned and said, "But it isn't even raining here." "That's exactly what makes it so dangerous," Faisal replied.

At breakfast, Faisal tried to explain, but his words were lost in the noise of cousins arriving and plates being passed around. When he finally got Grandfather's attention, the old man laughed kindly. "A cloud you cannot see, flooding a valley that is bone dry? You've been staring at that computer for too long!" A few of the cousins giggled, and Faisal felt his face burn, wishing he had kept quiet. Then he remembered a news report from the year before about a family whose car had been swept away in a flash flood.

Taking a deep breath, Faisal asked if he could speak to Grandfather alone. On the roof, he showed him the falling line on the graph and the dark shapes on the satellite map. "You always say a good shepherd watches the sky," he said quietly. "These are just my eyes, Grandfather, and they can see further than the horizon." The old man was silent for a long moment, studying the screen and then the distant mountains. "Your grandmother, may Allah have mercy on her, used to say that a wise man changes his mind, but a fool never does," he said at last.

Grandfather made a compromise: they would still have their picnic, but on a hill overlooking the wadi instead of on the valley floor. Some of the uncles grumbled, since the hill was rocky and had no shade, but nobody argued with Grandfather. By midday, the family had spread their carpets on the hilltop, and the smell of cardamom coffee filled the air. Below them, other groups had set up camp in the wadi itself, where the sand was soft and the trees were tall. Faisal kept glancing at the weather app on his phone, his stomach tight with worry.

In the middle of the afternoon, the wind suddenly changed direction, and the air began to smell of wet earth. Then they heard it: a deep, rumbling roar, like a lorry approaching from far away. "Look!" Noura cried, pointing up the valley. A wall of brown water, carrying branches and stones, was rushing towards the campsites below. Grandfather and the uncles shouted warnings and waved their arms, and the families in the wadi grabbed their children and ran for the slopes.

Within minutes, the spot where they had originally planned to sit had disappeared under a fast, muddy river. Thankfully, everyone had made it to safety, although one family's pickup truck had been carried several metres downstream. The people who had been camping below climbed up to join them, shaken and soaked, and the aunts immediately offered them dry blankets and hot tea. One of the fathers shook Faisal's hand firmly and said, "Your grandfather tells me we have you to thank." Faisal didn't know how to reply, so he simply poured the man another cup.

That evening, back home, Grandfather climbed the stairs to the roof slowly and carefully, leaning on his stick. He found Faisal checking the readings, which were rising again now that the storm had moved away. "So," the old man said with a smile, "what does your box say about tomorrow?" "Clear skies, Grandfather," Faisal replied. "Then perhaps tomorrow you can teach me how to read it," Grandfather said, sitting down beside him. Above them, the first stars appeared in a sky washed clean by the rain.

pages.text: The builders were due to arrive on Saturday, and by then the old majlis in Grandmother Noura's house in Abha would be covered in smooth grey plaster. Lina's father had been planning the renovation for months, and he was determined to make the house modern and comfortable. Lina had spent every summer of her fourteen years in that room, and she wasn't sure how she felt about it. On Thursday afternoon, while everyone else was packing boxes, she leaned against the wall and felt something strange under her fingers. A small flake of white paint had come loose, and beneath it was a flash of brilliant orange.

She glanced around to make sure no one was watching, then gently scratched at the edge with her fingernail. More colour appeared: a stripe of deep green, then a thin black line, then a triangle of sunflower yellow. Her heart began to race. She had seen patterns like this before, in a museum in Riyadh and on a poster at school. It looked exactly like Al-Qatt Al-Asiri, the traditional wall painting that women in the south of the Kingdom had created for generations.

"Baba, come and look at this!" she called, trying to keep her voice steady. Her father frowned, wiped his glasses and bent closer to the wall. "I had no idea there was anything under there," he admitted. "This room has been painted white for as long as I can remember." Grandmother Noura appeared in the doorway, leaning on her stick, and when she saw the patch of colour, she went completely still. "I always wondered whether anyone would find it," she said quietly.

That evening, over cardamom coffee and dates, Grandmother Noura told them the story. Her mother had painted the whole majlis when Noura was a girl, and Noura had helped by holding the brushes, which were made from goat hair. "Years later, when people started building concrete houses, many families thought the old patterns looked old-fashioned," she explained. "Your grandfather wanted the room to look modern, so we painted over everything. I regretted it the moment the last brushstroke was dry, but I never said a word."

Lina looked at her father, who was staring into his cup. "Baba, can't we delay the builders, just for a few days?" she begged. "If we uncover the wall carefully, perhaps it can still be saved." He hesitated, as he always did when time and money were involved. Then he looked at his mother's face and sighed. "Three days," he said at last. "If it's beyond repair, the plaster goes on as planned."

For three days, Lina hardly left the majlis. Following advice from a heritage conservation website, and with help from her cousin Faisal, who turned out to be surprisingly patient, she softened the paint with warm water and lifted it away with a plastic scraper, centimetre by centimetre. Slowly, the wall came back to life: rows of triangles, diamonds and zigzags in red, blue, green and yellow, running around the room like a bright necklace. By the second night, even her father had rolled up his sleeves and joined in. Nobody mentioned the builders anymore.

On the final afternoon, however, Lina noticed something puzzling. In the bottom corner near the window, one small triangle had never been painted at all; it was just bare plaster, surrounded by perfect colour. "Did the paint wash off here?" she asked, disappointed. Grandmother Noura smiled and shook her head. "No, habibti. My mother left that space empty on purpose, because she said a wall should always be waiting for the next pair of hands."

Lina felt a lump in her throat. "The next pair of hands... whose?" she asked, although she suspected she already knew the answer. Her grandmother reached into a cardboard box and took out a small tin wrapped in an old cloth. Inside were three brushes, their handles worn smooth, which she had kept hidden for over fifty years. "I was supposed to finish it, but I let the chance slip through my fingers," she said. "Perhaps it was meant for you all along."

Lina chose a rich green and, with her grandmother's hand resting gently on her wrist, she filled the empty triangle stroke by stroke. When the builders arrived on Saturday morning, her father asked them to repair the roof and leave the majlis exactly as it was. A few weeks later, a local newspaper photographed the restored wall, and Lina's art teacher invited her to give a talk at school. But the moment Lina treasured most came on her last evening in Abha, when she noticed a new triangle marked in pencil beside the one she had painted. "For the next pair of hands," her grandmother said, and they both laughed.

pages.text: Every fisherman on Farasan Island had heard the story of the ghost in the mangroves, but Faisal had always dismissed it as something adults told children to keep them away from the water at night. Then, one still morning in March, he saw it with his own eyes: a pale shape drifting between the twisted roots, rising and falling with the tide. His heart was pounding as he pushed his small boat closer. The shape wasn't a ghost at all. It was an enormous fishing net, grey with age, and caught inside it was a green sea turtle, struggling weakly.

"Hold on, little one," Faisal whispered, although the turtle was far too big to be called little. He pulled out the knife his uncle had given him and began cutting the thick nylon, strand by strand, careful not to touch the animal's flippers. It took him nearly twenty minutes, and by the end his fingers were bleeding. When the turtle finally slipped free, it hesitated for a moment, as if to thank him, and then disappeared into the blue. Faisal sat back in the boat, exhausted but grinning. Then he noticed something that wiped the smile off his face.

Further along the shore, more nets had wrapped themselves around the mangroves like grey spider webs. Tangled in them were the bones of fish, a seabird's feather, and the shell of a crab that would never move again. Faisal hauled one of the nets into the boat to show his uncle Ibrahim, who had fished these waters for thirty years. "Fishermen call them ghost nets," Uncle Ibrahim explained quietly, turning the net over in his rough hands. "When a net is lost or thrown away, it keeps on fishing for years, and nobody ever eats the catch."

That evening, Faisal couldn't stop thinking about what he had seen. He searched online and discovered that abandoned nets make up a huge proportion of the plastic in the world's oceans, and that they can take hundreds of years to break down. "We have to clean them up," he announced at dinner. His older sister Noura raised an eyebrow. "There must be kilometres of them out there, Faisal. Two people with a small boat would be a drop in the ocean."

But Faisal had made up his mind, and the next morning he was back among the mangroves before sunrise. To his surprise, Noura joined him an hour later, carrying gloves, a flask of tea and her phone. "If we're going to do this, we should do it properly," she said, and began photographing every net and recording its location on a map. By the end of the week, they had pulled out eleven nets, and Noura had noticed something interesting. Several of them had small orange plastic tags tied to the edges, each one marked with the same faded letters.

Faisal carried one of the tags home and placed it on the table in front of Uncle Ibrahim. "Do you recognise this?" he asked. His uncle's face changed, and for a long moment he said nothing. "That's my old mark," he admitted finally, rubbing his forehead. "Years ago, when a net got torn on the rocks, we just cut it loose and bought a new one. We didn't think about where it went."

Faisal had expected to feel angry, but instead he felt strangely sorry for his uncle, who looked older than Faisal had ever seen him. "You didn't know, Uncle," he said gently. "But now you do, and you know every fisherman on the island." Uncle Ibrahim looked at him for a long time, and then the corners of his mouth lifted. "You sound exactly like your grandfather," he said. "All right, let's see what an old man can do."

Within a month, things had begun to change. Uncle Ibrahim spoke to the fishermen after Friday prayers, and many of them, a little embarrassed, admitted they had done the same thing for years. They agreed to bring their damaged nets to a collection point at the harbour instead of leaving them in the sea, and Noura contacted a company in Jeddah that recycled old nylon into new products. Meanwhile, every weekend, boats full of volunteers, including fathers, sons, uncles and cousins, joined Faisal among the mangroves.

One evening in June, Faisal and Noura were sitting on the beach when a dark shape moved slowly out of the water towards the sand. It was a green turtle, and on her shell was a small scar exactly where a net might once have cut into it. Faisal couldn't be certain it was the same animal, but he chose to believe it was. They watched in silence as she dug a nest and laid her eggs in the moonlight. "Still think it's a drop in the ocean?" Faisal asked. Noura smiled and said, "Maybe, but the ocean is made of drops."

pages.text: Rakan had expected his summer in Abha to be a complete waste of time. Instead of hanging out with his friends in Riyadh, he had been sent to help his uncle Saeed in a tiny bookshop on a steep, foggy street. The shop smelled of dust and cardamom, and on most mornings hardly anyone came in. "Patience," his uncle kept saying, as he arranged the same shelves for the third time. "Books choose their readers slowly."

There was one customer, however, who came every Thursday without fail. He was an elderly man with a carefully trimmed white beard and a walking stick, and he always went straight to the poetry section. He would take down the same faded green book, sit in the corner chair, and stay there for nearly an hour. Then he would return it to the shelf, thank them politely, and leave without buying a thing. "He's been doing that for months," Rakan complained. "Why don't you just tell him it's not a library?"

Uncle Saeed looked at him over his glasses. "Some things are worth more than the price on the cover," he replied, but he refused to explain. The following Thursday, Rakan decided to pay closer attention. He noticed that the old man held the book unusually close to his face and that his finger moved slowly beneath each line. Sometimes he stopped on a page for so long that Rakan wondered whether he had fallen asleep.

It wasn't until the fourth week that it finally dawned on Rakan what was happening. As the man stood up, he bumped into a table and almost knocked over a pile of dictionaries. Rakan rushed over to help, and the man laughed with embarrassment. "Forgive me, my son," he said. "My eyes are not what they used to be, and the doctor says that soon I won't be able to read at all."

That evening, Rakan couldn't stop thinking about the green book. With his uncle's permission, he took it home and discovered that it was a collection of old poems about the mountains, the rain and the people of the south. Some of the words were difficult, but gradually he began to understand why someone might read them again and again. Then an idea struck him out of the blue. He borrowed his cousin's microphone, shut himself in his room, and started to record himself reading the poems aloud.

It was far harder than he had imagined. His voice cracked, the neighbour's goats kept interrupting, and he had to start some poems over a dozen times. By Wednesday night, though, he had recorded every single page. His uncle listened to a few minutes in silence, then put a hand on his shoulder. "You have gone the extra mile, Rakan," he said quietly, "and nobody even had to ask you."

On Thursday, the old man arrived as usual, but this time the green book was waiting for him on the counter, wrapped in brown paper with a small speaker beside it. Rakan explained, a little nervously, what he had done. For a long moment the man said nothing, and Rakan worried that he might have offended him. Then the man pressed play, and as Rakan's voice filled the shop, his eyes grew wet. "You have given me back something I thought I had lost forever," he whispered.

When Rakan refused to accept any money, the old man smiled and opened the book to its first page. "Do you know why I come here to read this particular book?" he asked. He pointed to a name printed beneath the title: Abdullah Al-Ghamdi. "Forty years ago, I wrote these poems," he said, "and your grandfather was the only bookseller brave enough to sell them." Rakan stared at him, completely lost for words.

Uncle Saeed had known all along, of course. For the rest of the summer, Abdullah came every Thursday, and Rakan read new poems to him while the old man shared stories about Abha in the old days. When it was finally time to return to Riyadh, Rakan realised he no longer considered the summer a waste. He had learned that kindness is rarely about grand gestures; more often, it begins with simply noticing someone. In his bag, carefully wrapped, was a faded green book of his own, signed by its author.

pages.text: For weeks, Layla had been begging her grandfather to take her kayaking in the mangroves of the Farasan Islands. Jaddi Saleh had spent thirty years in the coast guard, and he knew those twisting green channels better than anyone in the family. "The mangroves are beautiful, but they can be tricky," he warned her the night before. "Don't bite off more than you can chew." Layla, who was fourteen and felt perfectly capable of anything, just smiled and promised to listen.

They set off early the next afternoon, their double kayak sliding smoothly across the calm, turquoise water. As they paddled, Jaddi shared the lessons he had learned at sea. "The sea talks, if you are patient enough to listen," he said. "When the tide is going out, the water always flows towards the open sea, so it can show you the way home." Layla nodded politely, although she was more interested in the pink flamingos standing in the shallows.

Deep among the mangroves, Layla took dozens of photos of herons and crabs, and they completely lost track of time. When she finally looked up, she noticed that the bright sky had turned a strange, milky white. Within minutes, a thick fog had rolled in from the sea, swallowing the trees around them. "Stay calm," Jaddi said quietly, but she could hear the worry hidden in his voice. Every channel now looked exactly the same.

Trying to find a way out, they got stuck on a sandbank, and Jaddi climbed out to push the kayak free. Suddenly, his foot slipped on a hidden root, and he fell with a sharp cry of pain. By the time Layla had helped him back into his seat, his ankle was already swelling badly. She pulled out her phone to call her uncle, but there was no signal at all. For the first time that day, Layla felt genuinely afraid.

"You'll have to paddle us back, my dear," Jaddi said, his face pale. Layla took a deep breath and told herself to keep a cool head. She tried to remember everything he had told her earlier, words she had barely been paying attention to. Then she noticed a few dry leaves floating on the surface, drifting slowly but steadily in one direction. "The tide is going out," she whispered. "The water is showing us the way."

Layla followed the floating leaves, paddling harder than she had ever paddled before. However, the channel soon split into three narrow paths, and the current seemed to fade away completely. She chose the widest one, only to find that it led to a dead end blocked by fallen branches. Meanwhile, the water level was dropping fast, and if it fell much further, the kayak would be trapped in the mud until morning. Her arms ached, and the light was beginning to disappear.

Just as she was about to give up, a faint sound drifted through the fog. It was the Maghrib call to prayer, rising from the mosque in the fishing village near the harbour. Layla's heart leapt, because she knew the mosque stood right beside the beach where they had started. Turning the kayak until the sound was directly ahead of her, she chose the channel where the current felt strongest. Sound and water were pointing the same way at last.

Ten minutes later, the mangroves suddenly opened up, and the kayak glided out into wide, open water. Through the thinning fog, Layla spotted the swinging beam of a torch on a small fishing boat. "Over here!" she shouted, waving her paddle wildly above her head. It was her uncle Khalid, who had come looking for them when they hadn't returned. They had arrived in the nick of time, because the channel behind them was already turning to mud.

That evening, with his ankle wrapped in a bandage, Jaddi asked Layla how she had found the right path. When she mentioned the call to prayer, he laughed and shook his head in amazement. "I never taught you that trick," he admitted. "You worked it out all by yourself, which makes it far more valuable than anything I could have taught you." The next day, Layla drew a careful map of the mangroves, and beside the hidden channel that had saved them, Jaddi proudly wrote two words: Layla's Way.

pages.text: The ferry from Jazan cut through water so blue that Faisal could hardly believe it was real. He had come to the Farasan Islands to spend two weeks with his aunt Huda, a marine biologist who studied hawksbill turtles. "Don't expect a holiday," she warned him with a smile as she picked him up at the port. "We work at night, we sleep in the afternoon, and we never, ever leave rubbish on the sand." Faisal, who was fifteen and had never stayed up past midnight on purpose, nodded as if this were perfectly normal.

On his first night, they walked along a quiet beach with red torches, which turtles find less disturbing than white light. Aunt Huda knelt beside a small circle of sticks pushed into the sand. "About a hundred eggs are buried here," she whispered. "They were laid nearly two months ago, so they could hatch any night now." She explained that newborn turtles find the sea by crawling towards the brightest horizon, which is usually moonlight shining on the water. "For millions of years, that rule has worked perfectly," she added, "but people keep changing the rules."

The next morning, Faisal noticed something he had missed in the dark. Just behind the dunes, a brand-new café was almost finished, and workers were hanging long strings of bright white bulbs along its roof. A large sign announced the grand opening for Thursday evening. Faisal's stomach dropped, because Thursday was only two days away. "If those lights are switched on," he said slowly, "the baby turtles will think the café is the sea."

Aunt Huda immediately phoned the environmental office in Jazan, but the officer she needed was away until the following week. She wrote an official report, sent photos and left three messages, yet nobody replied. "These things take time," she sighed, rubbing her tired eyes. "Unfortunately, turtles don't wait for paperwork." Faisal paced up and down the small kitchen, feeling that they were running out of time.

That afternoon, without telling anyone, Faisal walked over to the café and asked to speak to the owner. Abu Saleh was a busy man with a phone in each hand, and at first he barely looked up. "Turtles?" he said, raising his eyebrows. "Young man, I've spent my savings on this place, and I need people to see it from the road." Faisal tried to explain about the nest and the moonlight, but the owner had already turned away to shout instructions at an electrician. Faisal left feeling foolish, wishing he had chosen his words more carefully.

On Wednesday night, a day earlier than anyone had expected, the sand inside the circle of sticks began to move. First one tiny flipper appeared, then a head, then dozens of small dark shapes pushed their way to the surface. At that exact moment, the café lights flashed on for a final test, and the whole beach glowed as if it were midday. To Faisal's horror, the hatchlings hesitated for a second and then turned away from the waves. One by one, they began crawling up the beach towards the dunes and the busy road beyond.

Faisal didn't stop to think; he simply ran. He burst into the café, where Abu Saleh was checking the decorations with his teenage son, Saleh. "Please, come and look, just for one minute!" Faisal begged, completely out of breath. Perhaps it was the panic in his voice, but the owner followed him outside. When he saw the trail of tiny turtles heading straight for the car park, his face changed completely, and he shouted to his son, "Switch everything off, now!"

Within seconds, the beach fell into darkness, and the silver line of moonlight on the sea became the brightest thing in sight again. Slowly, as if waking from a confusing dream, the hatchlings turned around. Aunt Huda, Faisal, Saleh and even Abu Saleh knelt on the sand, gently guiding the slowest ones with their red torches. For almost an hour, nobody said a word as the little turtles reached the wet sand and were carried away by the waves. "I had no idea," Abu Saleh finally murmured, shaking his head.

The café opened on Thursday after all, but it looked rather different from the plans. Abu Saleh had replaced the white bulbs with soft, low amber lights that turtles cannot easily see, and he had added a board explaining how visitors could protect the nests. A month later, back home in Riyadh, Faisal received a photo from Saleh showing the café's new name above the door: Hatchling Café. Underneath, Abu Saleh had written, "Thank you for not giving up on an old, stubborn man." Faisal smiled and realised that sometimes the bravest thing you can do is knock on a door twice.
