pages.text: Faris Al-Harbi had always believed that the sky above AlUla was the clearest in the world. On summer nights, when the heat finally faded from the sandstone cliffs, he would climb onto the roof with his grandfather and watch satellites crossing the stars like slow, silent sparks. His grandfather, a retired engineer, had kept an old amateur radio in a wooden cabinet for forty years. "Every voice you hear on this," he liked to say, "has travelled further than you think." Faris had never imagined that one day his own voice would be the one travelling upwards.

It all began with an announcement at school. Their science teacher, Mr Saleh, explained that the school had been selected for a live radio contact with the International Space Station. For roughly ten minutes, as the station passed overhead, students would be able to ask an astronaut questions directly. Because Faris had been helping his grandfather set up antennas for years, he was chosen to operate the radio during the contact. He spent the next three weeks practising call signs, checking cables and rehearsing questions until he could have recited them in his sleep.

The contact was scheduled for 8:42 p.m. on a Thursday, and by seven o'clock the school courtyard was packed with families. Parents sat in long rows of chairs, younger children waved small flags, and a local news team had set up a camera. Faris checked the antenna for the hundredth time, his stomach tight with nerves. His grandfather sat quietly near the back, his walking stick resting against his knee. Then, without warning, a hot wind rose from the desert, carrying a thick cloud of dust towards the school.

Within minutes, the dust storm had swallowed the lights of the town. Somewhere nearby a power line must have been damaged, because every lamp in the courtyard flickered and went out. The crowd fell silent, and then a hundred phone screens lit up in the darkness. Mr Saleh rushed over, his face pale. "The school generator won't start," he said. "Unless we find power in the next twenty minutes, we'll miss the station completely."

Faris felt as if weeks of preparation were about to be blown away by the wind. Then his grandfather placed a firm hand on his shoulder. "Don't lose hope so quickly," he said calmly, "because my old radio doesn't need the school's electricity — it runs perfectly well on a car battery." Faris stared at him in disbelief, pointing out that the radio was older than his own father. The old man simply smiled and replied, "Exactly, which is why it has survived far worse than a little dust."

What followed was a race against the clock. Faris's uncle drove the car as close to the courtyard as he could, while two older students carried the heavy wooden radio from the boot. With dust stinging their eyes, Faris and his grandfather connected the cables to the battery by torchlight. Luckily, the school's modern antenna was still standing, so they attached it to the old set. At 8:40, the radio crackled into life, hissing like a kettle about to boil.

At exactly 8:42, Faris pressed the button and spoke into the microphone, repeating the call sign he had practised so many times. For a few seconds there was only static, and he was sure they had failed. Then a calm voice cut through the noise: "This is the International Space Station. We hear you loud and clear." The courtyard exploded with cheers, and Faris had to wave his arms to make everyone quiet again. One after another, students stepped forward to ask about sleeping without gravity, growing plants in orbit, and what Earth looked like at night.

With less than a minute left, Faris asked the final question, which he had written himself. "What can you see right now?" After a short pause, the astronaut replied, "Actually, I can see a huge brown cloud stretching across northwest Arabia." He added with a laugh that someone down there was clearly having a very windy evening. Laughter swept through the dark courtyard, and then the voice faded into static as the station disappeared over the horizon.

Later that night, after the power had returned and the families had gone home, Faris sat on the roof with his grandfather once more. The storm had passed, and the sky had been washed clean, glittering with more stars than he could count. "You were right," Faris said. "Voices really do travel further than you think." His grandfather pointed to a small light moving steadily across the sky. "Yes," he said proudly, "and tonight, so did yours."

pages.text: Faisal Al-Harbi was famous at his school in Jeddah for one thing: his voice. As captain of the under-15 team, he could be heard from the car park, shouting instructions, warnings and encouragement at anyone who would listen. "Faisal doesn't need a whistle," Coach Nasser liked to joke. "He is the whistle." With the regional cup final only four days away, nobody could have predicted that this voice was about to disappear.

On Saturday morning, he woke up with a throat that felt as if it had been scraped with sandpaper. When he tried to say good morning to his mother, only a dry whisper came out. The doctor at the clinic examined him and shook her head. "It's laryngitis," she said. "If you want your voice back, you must rest it completely: no talking, and definitely no shouting, for at least a week." Faisal stared at her in horror, because the final was on Wednesday.

That evening he sat on the sofa feeling sorry for himself, typing angry messages on his phone. His younger cousin Hamad, who had been deaf since birth, was visiting with his parents. Hamad watched him for a while, then signed something to his father, who laughed. "He says you look like a lion that has lost its roar," his uncle translated. Faisal frowned, but then an idea struck him: if Hamad could say so much without a single sound, perhaps a captain could too.

The next day, Faisal turned up at training with Hamad and a notebook full of sketches. Coach Nasser was doubtful at first, but he agreed to give the plan a chance. Together, the cousins taught the team a set of simple hand signals: a closed fist meant "hold your position", two fingers pointing forward meant "press higher", and a flat hand moving down meant "slow the game". Some of the boys found it awkward and kept forgetting, while others treated it like a secret code from a spy film. By the end of the session, even Omar, the team's biggest sceptic, had to admit it was working.

Over the next two days, something unexpected happened. Because Faisal couldn't shout, everyone had to keep their heads up and look at one another constantly. The defenders began talking to each other more, and the midfielders started to anticipate each other's movements. "I used to wait for you to tell me what to do," admitted Ziyad, the shy left-back. "Now I actually have to think for myself." Faisal grinned and gave him a thumbs-up, which needed no translation.

On Wednesday afternoon, the stadium was packed with families, and the noise from the stands was deafening. Their opponents, Al-Noor Academy, were bigger and faster, and they had not lost a match all season. Within ten minutes, they had taken the lead with a powerful header from a corner. Faisal felt the old urge to scream at his team, but he swallowed it. Instead, he raised a calm, flat hand and lowered it slowly: slow down, stay together.

Gradually, his team regained control. Al-Noor's players communicated by shouting, but in the roar of the crowd, half their instructions were lost. Faisal's team, meanwhile, didn't need to hear anything; they only needed to look. Just before half-time, Faisal signalled with two fingers, and the whole team pressed high at once, catching Al-Noor's defenders off guard. Omar stole the ball and slotted it into the bottom corner to make it 1-1.

The second half was tense, and as the minutes ticked away, both teams were running on empty. Then, in the final minute, Faisal spotted a gap on the left wing. He couldn't call for Ziyad, so he simply caught his eye and pointed. Ziyad sprinted forward, received the pass and crossed the ball perfectly into the box. Faisal threw himself at it, and the ball flew past the goalkeeper into the net.

When the final whistle blew, his teammates lifted him onto their shoulders, cheering loudly enough for all of them. Up in the stands, Hamad was jumping up and down, signing something over and over. Faisal laughed and signed back the first phrase his cousin had ever taught him: "Thank you, brother." That evening, as he held the trophy, he realised that he had learned something more valuable than a victory. Sometimes the best leaders aren't the loudest people on the pitch; they're the ones who help everyone else find their own voice.

pages.text: For three weeks, Yusuf had been giving Hamza the cold shoulder. They had been inseparable since primary school, sharing everything from football boots to exam nerves, so the silence felt heavier than any argument. It had all started with a video: a clip of Yusuf tripping over his own feet during a class presentation, slowed down and set to silly music. Within minutes, it had spread through the class group chat, and the account that posted it belonged to Hamza. When Hamza tried to explain, Yusuf simply walked away, too humiliated to listen.

So when Mr. Al-Harbi announced the pairs for the school hiking trip to Jebel Fihrayn, known as the Edge of the World, Yusuf's heart sank. "Yusuf and Hamza," the teacher read, without looking up from his clipboard. A few boys exchanged knowing glances. Yusuf considered asking for a change, but his pride wouldn't let him. "Fine," he muttered, though it was anything but fine.

The bus left Riyadh early in the morning, and by late afternoon the group was walking along the cliffs, where the land suddenly dropped hundreds of metres to the plain below. Hamza tried twice to start a conversation, but Yusuf kept his eyes fixed on the path. Determined to prove he didn't need anyone, Yusuf took a narrower trail to photograph an unusual rock formation, and Hamza, sighing, followed him. By the time they turned back, the rest of the class had disappeared over the ridge. The sun was sinking fast, and neither of their phones had a signal.

"We should have stayed with the group," Hamza said quietly. Yusuf opened his mouth to snap back, then bit his tongue, because Hamza was right. As they hurried down a rocky slope, Yusuf's foot slipped and he landed hard, gasping as pain shot through his ankle. Hamza was beside him in an instant, kneeling in the dust. "Don't move," he said. "Let me have a look."

Hamza had taken a first-aid course the previous summer, and he worked calmly, wrapping Yusuf's ankle tightly with a bandage from his backpack. Watching him, Yusuf felt a strange mixture of gratitude and guilt. "Why are you helping me?" he asked at last. "I've been horrible to you." Hamza tied the bandage and looked up. "Because you're my friend, even if you've forgotten it."

Darkness fell, and with it came a sharp desert chill. They had no idea which direction the camp lay in, but Yusuf, leaning against a boulder, noticed the stars appearing one by one. His grandfather had spent countless nights teaching him to find Al-Jadi, the North Star, just as travellers across the Arabian Peninsula had done for centuries. "The camp is north of the cliffs," he said, pointing upwards. "If we keep that star in front of us, we'll reach it." For the first time in weeks, Hamza smiled at him.

They moved slowly, Yusuf's arm over Hamza's shoulder, and somewhere along the way the silence between them finally broke. "About the video," Hamza began. "My cousin Majed was staying with us that weekend, and he borrowed my phone and posted it as a joke. I deleted it the moment I saw it, but by then everyone had already shared it." Yusuf stopped walking. "Why didn't you tell me?" "I tried," Hamza said simply. "You never let me finish a sentence."

Yusuf felt his face burn with shame. He had been so certain, so quick to judge, that he had never once considered that Hamza might be innocent. "I'm sorry," he said, and the words, which had seemed impossible for weeks, came out easily. "I should have trusted you. If I'd listened, we could have cleared the air ages ago." Hamza shrugged, grinning. "Well, you can make it up to me by never taking a shortcut again."

An hour later, they saw torches flickering ahead and heard Mr. Al-Harbi calling their names. The teacher's relief quickly turned into a long lecture about safety, which both boys accepted without complaint. Later, wrapped in blankets beside the fire, Yusuf found a weak signal on his phone and typed a message to the class group: "Hamza didn't post that video. He's the best friend anyone could ask for." Then he looked up at Al-Jadi, still shining steadily above them, and thought that some things, like stars and true friends, are easiest to find in the dark.

pages.text: Faris had always believed that almost any problem could be solved with a fully charged phone. So when his grandfather announced that he would take Faris and his cousin Yousef camping in the Nafud desert for three days, Faris downloaded four different map apps before they had even left Ha'il. "The desert doesn't care about your apps," Grandfather Saleh said with a smile as he loaded water containers into his old Land Cruiser. Faris laughed politely, but secretly he thought the old man was a little out of date.

For two days, the trip was everything Faris had hoped for. They cooked rice over a crackling fire, drank cardamom coffee, and followed the delicate tracks of a desert fox until they disappeared behind a dune. At night, Grandfather pointed out the stars, naming each one as though it were an old friend. "That one is Al-Jadi, the North Star," he explained. "Travellers in this land have trusted it for thousands of years." Yousef listened carefully, but Faris was too busy holding his phone in the air, hoping to catch enough signal to upload his photos.

On the third morning, they drove deeper into the sand to find a well that Grandfather remembered from his youth. Around noon, the sky turned a strange, sickly yellow, and the horizon began to blur. "Sandstorm," Grandfather said quietly, and he stopped the car at once. Within minutes, a wall of sand had swallowed the dunes, and the wind was howling like an angry animal. For hours they sat in the car with scarves over their faces, unable to see more than a metre beyond the windows.

By the time the storm had finally died down, it was late afternoon and the car was half-buried in sand. Worse still, the engine refused to start, no matter how many times Grandfather turned the key. Faris pulled out his phone and felt his stomach drop: there was no signal, the battery was at nine percent, and the map showed nothing but an empty grey screen. Grandfather, however, remained completely calm. "Your father's camp is about fifteen kilometres east," he said. "We'll walk once the sun goes down, because in this heat the sun would defeat us long before the distance did."

While they waited in the shade of the car, Grandfather taught them how to read the land. "The wind here usually blows from the same direction, so the dunes line up like waves on the sea," he explained, tracing their shape in the sand with his finger. "Learn their pattern, and they become a map." For the first time, Faris put his phone away and paid attention. Then, as they began climbing the first dune at sunset, Grandfather's foot slipped on the loose sand, and he fell with a sharp cry of pain.

His ankle was badly twisted, and he could only move slowly, leaning heavily on Yousef's shoulder. "Faris, you'll have to lead us," Grandfather said, his face tight with pain. Faris's heart sank, because without a screen to guide him he felt completely blind. Then, as the first stars appeared, he remembered the bright, steady light his grandfather had shown him. If the North Star was there, then east had to be on his right. He took a deep breath, lined himself up with the waves of sand, and stepped forward.

They walked for hours, stopping regularly so that Grandfather could rest his ankle. Every few minutes, Faris checked the star and the direction of the dunes, just to make sure they hadn't drifted off course. At one point, Yousef grabbed his arm and insisted that he could see lights far to the south. Faris hesitated, tempted to turn, but then he recalled his grandfather's warning that tired eyes often play tricks in the desert. "We keep going east," he said firmly, and Grandfather squeezed his shoulder. "Now," the old man whispered proudly, "you are reading the desert."

Just before dawn, Faris caught the faint smell of woodsmoke drifting across the sand. Moments later, a pair of headlights swept over the top of a dune, and a familiar voice called out their names. It was Faris's father, who had been searching with two friends ever since the storm had ended. He hugged all three of them so tightly that Yousef complained he couldn't breathe. "How on earth did you find your way?" his father asked, and Grandfather simply nodded towards Faris.

Back home in Ha'il, Faris plugged in his phone, but the first thing he did was buy a small notebook. On its first page, he carefully drew the North Star and the shape of the dunes, exactly as his grandfather had taught him. "So, will you delete all your map apps now?" Grandfather teased him. Faris grinned and shook his head. "No, but from now on I'll never trust them more than I trust the sky."

pages.text: Yousef had always believed that technology could solve any problem, including his grandfather. Grandpa Saleh still kept a paper diary, wound his watch every morning and wrote phone numbers on the back of his hand. So when his parents announced that the whole family would gather at Grandpa's house for Eid lunch, Yousef saw his chance. "This year," he told his younger sister Lama, "I'm going to drag Grandpa into the twenty-first century." Lama, who was eleven and far too wise for her age, simply raised an eyebrow.

Two days before Eid, Yousef arrived with a small grey speaker and a box of smart light bulbs. He spent the afternoon changing bulbs, climbing onto the roof to fix the internet cable and naming the assistant "Noor", because Grandpa liked the word. "You just talk to her," he explained proudly. "Say 'Noor, turn on the lights,' and she does it immediately." Grandpa leaned towards the speaker as if it were a nervous kitten and boomed, "NOOR, TURN ON THE LIGHTS!"

The lights stayed off. Instead, a calm voice replied, "Adding forty kilos of lemons to your shopping basket." Yousef grabbed his phone and cancelled the order, his ears turning bright red. "She's just getting used to your voice," he insisted. Grandpa nodded seriously and asked about the weather, but Noor set an alarm for four o'clock in the morning and announced that it would repeat every day "until further notice".

By the next morning, things had gone from bad to worse. The alarm had woken the entire street, and the neighbour's cat had been spotted on the roof, refusing to come down. When Grandpa asked Noor to call his brother Hamad, she played ten minutes of camel noises instead. Grandma, who had been preparing the kabsa since dawn, came out of the kitchen holding a wooden spoon. "Yousef," she said sweetly, which was always a bad sign, "if that machine speaks again before lunch, it will be sleeping in the garden."

Yousef was determined not to give up. He sat at the kitchen table for hours, adjusting settings, watching tutorials and muttering to himself. Lama brought him a cup of tea and watched with obvious enjoyment. "Have you considered," she said, "that maybe the problem isn't Grandpa?" Yousef didn't bother to reply, mainly because he was starting to wonder the same thing.

On Eid day, the house filled up with uncles, aunts, cousins and a mountain of dates. Everything was going smoothly until Uncle Majid, curious about the speaker, asked loudly, "Noor, what was Yousef's latest search?" Before Yousef could dive across the room, Noor answered clearly: "How to make Grandpa think I am a genius." There was a moment of silence, and then the whole room burst out laughing at once. Yousef wished the ground would open up and swallow him whole.

Just then, the doorbell rang. A delivery man stood outside, sweating, next to a tower of boxes. "Forty kilos of lemons for Mr Saleh," he announced. Yousef turned pale. "But I cancelled that order! I definitely cancelled it!" Behind him, Grandpa cleared his throat and calmly took out his own phone.

"You cancelled it," Grandpa said, his eyes twinkling, "so I ordered them again myself." He explained that he had been using a smartphone for three years, made video calls to his old friends in Jeddah and even paid his bills online. "While you were up on the roof fixing that cable, I connected Noor to my phone and changed a few settings," he admitted. "My grandson came to teach me, and I didn't have the heart to tell him I already knew. Besides, I wanted to see how far he would go." Across the room, Lama looked at Yousef and silently mouthed, "I told you."

The camel noises, it turned out, had been Grandpa's idea too, and he still thought they were hilarious. Yousef laughed until his stomach hurt, partly from relief and partly because he had been well and truly fooled. That afternoon, Grandma turned the lemons into jugs of fresh lemon and mint juice, and everyone agreed it was the best Eid drink they had ever tasted. Before leaving, Yousef hugged his grandfather and asked what he should teach him next year. "Next year," Grandpa replied with a grin, "I'll be teaching you."

Let me start by telling you why I love chess.
Let me to start by telling you why I love chess.
Let me start by tell you why I love chess.

2-4.answer: According to the chart, most teenagers sleep less than eight hours.
There was a sharp rise in gaming time during the holidays.

2-4.q: There was a slight drop ___ the number of teens who read every day.
options: of
in
on

2-4.q: Reading time fell by 30%. This suggests ___
options: that teens are spending more time on screens.
teens to spend more time on screens.
that teens spending more time on screens.
The chart shows a sharply rise in screen time.
The chart is showing a sharp raise of screen time.
The chart shows a sharp rise in screen time.

2-5.answer: The idea behind this project is to create a school garden.
This would benefit younger students by giving them a quiet place to read.

2-5.q: Audience member: "Won't this project cost a lot of money?" Choose the best reply.
options: No, it won't. Next question.
That's a great question — what I mean is we'll use recycled materials, so costs stay low.
I don't know, it's not my problem.

2-5.q: This would benefit the local community ___ reducing litter in the park.
options: by
for
with
This project would benefits elderly people by help them with shopping.
This project will benefit to elderly people by helping them shopping.
This project would benefit elderly people by helping them with shopping.

words.ex: My parents are trying to limit my screen time to two hours a day.
Some apps are designed to be addictive, so it's hard to stop scrolling.
My phone is a huge distraction when I'm trying to do my homework.
Social media helps me keep in touch with my cousins who live abroad.
Comparing yourself to influencers online can affect your mental health.
I sometimes scroll through videos for an hour without noticing.

dialogue.t: Do you think teenagers spend too much time on their phones?
While it's true that phones are useful, I'd argue that most of us use them far too much.
Really? Why do you say that?
The main reason I feel this way is that I lose hours scrolling through videos instead of sleeping.
I know what you mean. Not only does it keep me up late, but it also makes me tired in class.
Exactly. And social media can be really addictive, especially with all the notifications.
Still, I use it to keep in touch with my friends, so I don't think it's all bad.
That's fair. Maybe the problem isn't the phone, it's how much screen time we allow ourselves.

grammar.title: Not only ... but also (with inversion)
grammar.ar: نستخدم تركيب Not only ... but also لإضافة فكرة ثانية تقوّي الفكرة الأولى، وهو أسلوب مفيد جدًا في الإقناع. عندما نبدأ الجملة بـ Not only يجب أن نقلب ترتيب الفاعل والفعل كما في السؤال، فنقول: Not only does it ... وليس Not only it does. في الجزء الثاني نستخدم but ... also مع الترتيب العادي للجملة.
examples: Not only does social media waste time, but it also affects our sleep.
Not only is my phone useful for school, but it also helps me relax.
Not only do teenagers check their phones constantly, but they also feel anxious without them.

words.ex: The head teacher's proposal is to make the school day one hour longer.
It would be difficult for teachers to enforce a total phone ban.
She listened carefully and then gave a strong counterargument.
A good compromise would be allowing phones only during breaks.
Students can't concentrate properly when their phones keep buzzing.
Wouldn't a more flexible timetable suit everyone better?

dialogue.t: I think the school should ban phones in class completely. They're nothing but a distraction.
I see your point, but have you considered that we sometimes use phones to look up information?
That may be the case, however most students just end up chatting with friends.
Some do, but wouldn't it be better if teachers decided when phones could be used?
Hmm, that sounds like a lot of work to enforce. A total ban is simpler.
Simpler, maybe, but a ban doesn't teach us to use technology responsibly.
That's a good counterargument. So what compromise would you suggest?
Phones stay in our bags unless the teacher says we need them for a task.

grammar.title: Polite suggestions: Wouldn't it be better if + past simple
grammar.ar: نستخدم السؤال المنفي Wouldn't it be better if ...? لتقديم اقتراح بطريقة مهذبة وغير مباشرة أثناء النقاش. بعد if نستخدم الماضي البسيط رغم أننا نتحدث عن الحاضر أو المستقبل، لأن الموقف افتراضي وليس حقيقيًا بعد. لا نتوقع إجابة بنعم أو لا، بل نريد أن يفكّر الطرف الآخر في فكرتنا.
examples: Wouldn't it be better if we had longer breaks instead of longer days?
Wouldn't it be better if students helped write the school rules?
Wouldn't it be better if phones were collected at the start of each exam?

words.ex: Online learning offers flexibility because you can study at your own pace.
You need a lot of self-discipline to study at home without a teacher.
I prefer face-to-face lessons because I can ask questions immediately.
Group work in class encourages interaction between students.
Some students felt a sense of isolation during months of online school.
The main drawback of online classes is poor internet connection.

dialogue.t: So, which do you prefer: online learning or being in a real classroom?
On the one hand, online learning gives you flexibility. On the other hand, it's easy to get distracted at home.
True. Whereas online learning lets you rewatch lessons, classroom learning gives you instant feedback.
And there's more interaction in class. I felt a bit of isolation when we studied online.
Me too, although I liked not having to wake up so early!
Ha, that's one advantage. But you need real self-discipline to keep up.
All things considered, I'd say a mix of both is the best option.
I agree. Face-to-face for most lessons, and online for extra practice.

grammar.title: Linking contrasting ideas: whereas / on the one hand ... on the other hand
grammar.ar: نستخدم whereas لربط جملتين تحملان فكرتين متعارضتين داخل جملة واحدة، ويمكن وضعها في بداية الجملة أو وسطها. أما On the one hand ... On the other hand فنستخدمها لعرض جانبين لموضوع واحد، وغالبًا في جملتين منفصلتين. هذه الأدوات تجعل حديثك متوازنًا ومنظّمًا، وهو أمر مهم في امتحانات المحادثة.
examples: Whereas online learning is flexible, classroom learning is more social.
On the one hand, online classes save travel time. On the other hand, they can feel lonely.
My brother loves studying online, whereas I learn better with a teacher in the room.

words.ex: There's growing evidence that sugary drinks are linked to health problems.
Childhood obesity has increased in many countries over the last twenty years.
Many fast food adverts target children with toys and cartoon characters.
It's misleading to call a burger meal 'healthy' just because it includes salad.
Stricter regulation of advertising could protect young people.
Teenagers are an important group of consumers for fast food companies.

dialogue.t: Do you think there should be stricter rules on fast food adverts for young people?
Definitely. There's growing evidence that these adverts make children want unhealthy food.
Maybe, but it could be argued that parents, not adverts, decide what kids eat.
Parents matter, of course. But companies target teenagers on social media, where parents can't see.
That's true. Some adverts are quite misleading too, showing burgers as if they were healthy.
Exactly. If we don't introduce some regulation, there's a risk that obesity rates will keep rising.
I still think banning all adverts goes too far, though.
Fair enough, but at least they shouldn't be shown during children's programmes.

grammar.title: First conditional for warnings: If we don't ..., there's a risk that ...
grammar.ar: نستخدم الشرط الأول للحديث عن نتيجة محتملة في المستقبل إذا حدث (أو لم يحدث) شيء ما. نستخدم المضارع البسيط بعد if، ثم will أو تعبيرًا مثل there's a risk that في الجزء الثاني. هذا التركيب قوي في النقاش لأنه يُحذّر المستمع من نتائج سلبية. انتبه: لا نستخدم will بعد if مباشرة.
examples: If we don't limit these adverts, there's a risk that children will eat more junk food.
If schools don't teach healthy eating, students won't understand the dangers.
If the government introduces stricter rules, companies will have to change their marketing.

words.ex: He conceded that e-sports require skill, but he didn't change his mind.
She maintained her position even when everyone disagreed with her.
Football requires a lot more physical effort than playing video games.
Professional gamers need incredibly fast reflexes.
That's a fair point; I hadn't thought about the training schedules.
We both love sport, but we see it differently when it comes to gaming.

dialogue.t: Honestly, I don't think e-sports should be called real sport. You're just sitting in a chair!
But pro gamers train for hours every day and need amazing reflexes.
I'll admit that they're very skilled, but I still believe sport needs real physical effort.
Chess is recognised as a sport in some places, and that's not physical either.
You've got a point there, although chess has been around for centuries.
So age makes something a sport? E-sports have huge competitions and millions of fans.
Popular, yes, but popularity doesn't make it a sport. Let's just say we see it differently because we define sport in different ways.
Fair enough. Let's agree to disagree, then!

grammar.title: Conceding and contrasting: I'll admit that ..., but I still ... / although
grammar.ar: في النقاش الحاد، من الأدب أن تعترف بنقطة صحيحة عند الطرف الآخر ثم تعود إلى رأيك. نستخدم I'll admit that ... أو You've got a point للاعتراف، ثم but ... still أو although لإظهار أنك ما زلت متمسكًا بموقفك. كلمة still تعني أن رأيك لم يتغير رغم ما سمعته. لاحظ أن although تربط جملتين ولا تُستخدم معها but في الجملة نفسها.
examples: I'll admit that gaming takes practice, but I still don't see it as a sport.
You've got a point there, although not everyone would agree.
Although e-sports are exciting to watch, I still prefer traditional sports.

words.ex: Today's motion is: 'Homework should be banned for students under 16.'
My opponent made some good points, but her evidence was weak.
In your rebuttal, you should respond to the other team's main argument.
I'm firmly against the idea of making school uniforms optional.
Her closing summary was so convincing that she won the debate.
Some people claim that homework improves results, but studies disagree.

dialogue.t: The motion is: 'Homework should be banned for students under 16.' I'm firmly in favour of this motion because students need time to rest and enjoy hobbies.
Thank you. I'm firmly against it because homework helps us practise what we learn in class.
My opponent claims that homework helps us practise, yet many students just copy answers online.
My opponent claims that students need rest, yet without homework many would simply spend more time on their phones.
That may be true for some, but it's not a reason to give everyone extra work.
To sum up, the strongest argument is that regular practice at home leads to better learning.
To sum up, the strongest argument is that tired, stressed students can't learn effectively at all.
Well, it was a convincing debate. Let's see what the audience decides!

grammar.title: Reporting and challenging claims: claim that ..., yet ...
grammar.ar: في المناظرة، نحتاج إلى نقل كلام الخصم قبل الرد عليه. نستخدم أفعال النقل مثل claim, argue, suggest متبوعة بـ that ثم جملة كاملة. الفعل claim يُلمّح إلى أننا نشك في صحة الكلام. بعد ذلك نستخدم yet (بمعنى ومع ذلك/لكن) لتقديم الحجة المضادة بشكل قوي.
examples: My opponent claims that uniforms are unfair, yet they actually reduce pressure to wear expensive clothes.
The other team argues that homework is essential, yet top-performing countries give very little.
Some people suggest that social media is harmless, yet many teenagers report feeling anxious.

words.ex: She gave such a vivid description of the desert that I could almost feel the heat.
He paused for a moment to build suspense before telling us who had won.
The view of the rock formations in AlUla at sunset was absolutely breathtaking.
We were chatting quietly when, all of a sudden, the lights went out.
Waiting for the judges to announce the results was really nerve-racking.
Our family Eid gathering last year was unforgettable because all my cousins came from abroad.

dialogue.t: So, how was your trip to AlUla? You've been really quiet about it.
Honestly, it was amazing. We had been walking through the canyon for hours when suddenly we heard a strange echo behind us.
No way! What was it?
Well, just as we were about to turn back, a group of camels came around the corner. My little brother screamed so loudly!
Ha! That must have been terrifying for him. Were they wild?
That's what we thought. It was only later that I realised they belonged to a guide who was leading a tour nearby.
That's hilarious. You should tell that story in class — it's got real suspense.
Maybe I will. I'll just leave out the part where I almost screamed too!

grammar.title: Narrative Tenses for Suspense
grammar.ar: نستخدم الماضي التام المستمر (had been + فعل ing) لوصف نشاط استمر فترة قبل أن يقطعه حدث مفاجئ في الماضي البسيط. وتعني عبارة Just as we were about to أننا كنا على وشك فعل شيء ما عندما حدث أمر آخر. أما It was only later that I realised فتُستخدم لكشف حقيقة لم نفهمها إلا بعد وقوع الأحداث، وهي تضيف عنصر المفاجأة إلى القصة.
examples: I had been practising my speech for hours when suddenly my laptop crashed.
Just as we were about to leave the house, my grandmother arrived with a huge tray of sweets.
It was only later that I realised I had left my phone at the competition hall.

words.ex: You need to roast the coffee beans lightly to get the traditional Saudi flavour.
My grandfather always grinds the cardamom by hand instead of using a machine.
Let the coffee brew for about ten minutes before you pour it.
The video explains step by step how to set up your account.
My favourite feature of this app is that it reminds me to drink water.
It's essential to save your work regularly, otherwise you might lose everything.

dialogue.t: I want to make Saudi coffee for my friends this weekend, but I've never done it. Can you explain how?
Sure, it's easier than it looks. The first step is to roast the beans until they're light golden.
Light golden? I thought coffee was supposed to be dark.
Not Saudi coffee. Once that's done, you grind the beans and boil them in water for about ten minutes.
Okay, and when do I add the cardamom?
Add it right at the end. It's essential to take the pot off the heat first, otherwise the cardamom will lose its aroma.
Got it. Is there anything else I should know?
Just remember to serve it in small cups with dates. That's the whole experience!

grammar.title: Sequencing and Giving Warnings
grammar.ar: عند شرح عملية ما، نستخدم كلمات الترتيب مثل The first step is to ثم Once that's done لربط الخطوات بشكل واضح ومنطقي. وتأتي بعد The first step is to صيغة المصدر (to + الفعل). ونستخدم It's essential to ... otherwise ... لنوضح خطوة مهمة جداً ونبيّن النتيجة السلبية إذا لم نقم بها.
examples: The first step is to download the app and create a free account.
Once that's done, you can choose the topics you're interested in.
It's essential to turn on notifications, otherwise you'll miss your daily reminders.

words.ex: My older sister has always been a role model for me because she works so hard.
Her determination helped her finish the marathon even though she was injured.
Failing his first exam was a setback, but he didn't give up.
He overcame his fear of public speaking by practising every day.
Despite being famous, the scientist remained humble and kind to everyone.
My grandfather has had a huge influence on the way I treat other people.

dialogue.t: For the project, I'm going to talk about my uncle. He's a doctor who works in rural areas.
That sounds interesting. Why did you choose him?
Well, what I admire most about him is his patience. He never rushes his patients, even when he's exhausted.
Was it difficult for him to become a doctor?
Very. Despite growing up in a small village with no proper school, he managed to get a scholarship to study medicine.
Wow, that's real determination. How has he influenced you?
He has taught me that where you start doesn't decide where you finish. That really motivates me.
That's a powerful message. I think everyone will remember your talk.

grammar.title: Emphasis with 'What' Clauses and 'Despite'
grammar.ar: نستخدم تركيب What I admire most about ... is ... لإبراز صفة معيّنة وجعلها محور الجملة، وهو أقوى من قول I admire his patience فقط. أما Despite فيأتي بعدها اسم أو فعل بصيغة ing، ولا يأتي بعدها فاعل وفعل مباشرةً، فنقول Despite growing up ولا نقول Despite he grew up. ونستخدم المضارع التام في He has taught me that لأن أثر الشخص ما زال مستمراً حتى الآن.
examples: What I admire most about my mother is her ability to stay calm under pressure.
Despite her injury, she managed to win a silver medal at the championship.
My coach has taught me that losing is just another chance to learn.

words.ex: Start your talk with a surprising fact as a hook to grab the audience's attention.
In the introduction, briefly outline the three points you'll cover.
Asking a question at the start is a great way to engage the audience.
Each main point should have one clear example to support it.
Try to make eye contact with different people while you're speaking.
Let's wrap up the meeting by summarising what we've agreed on.

dialogue.t: Can you listen to my talk and give me feedback? It's about falconry.
Of course. Go ahead, I'm timing you.
Today I'd like to talk about falconry, a hobby that connects me to my family's heritage. Let me start by explaining how I first got involved.
Nice opening. Keep going.
...so that's how my grandfather trained his first falcon. Moving on to the skills you need, the most important one is patience.
To wrap up, falconry isn't just a sport — it's a way of keeping our traditions alive. Thank you for listening.
That was exactly two minutes! Your structure was really clear, but try to make more eye contact next time.
Thanks, I kept looking at my notes. I'll practise it a few more times.

grammar.title: Signposting Language in Presentations
grammar.ar: عبارات الإرشاد (signposting) تساعد المستمع على متابعة أجزاء العرض: المقدمة والجسم والخاتمة. نستخدم Today I'd like to talk about لتقديم الموضوع، ويأتي بعد Let me start by فعل بصيغة ing. ونستخدم Moving on to للانتقال إلى فكرة جديدة، ويأتي بعدها اسم أو فعل بصيغة ing، ثم To wrap up لتلخيص الأفكار وإنهاء العرض.
examples: Today I'd like to talk about why I love photography.
Let me start by showing you the first photo I ever took.
Moving on to the equipment, you don't actually need an expensive camera to begin.

words.ex: There was a sharp rise in the number of teens using social media at night.
The chart shows a slight drop in reading time between 2020 and 2023.
Over half of the respondents said they sleep less than seven hours a night.
Time spent gaming increased gradually over the five-year period.
The number of students who exercise daily remained steady throughout the year.
There is a significant difference between how much boys and girls read.

dialogue.t: Let's look at this chart about teenagers' sleep. What do you notice first?
According to the chart, most teens slept around eight hours a night in 2019.
Right, but look at what happened after that.
There was a slight drop in 2020, and then a sharp rise in screen time at night in 2021.
And sleep went down to about six and a half hours. That's a significant change.
This suggests that phones and gaming are affecting how much teens sleep.
I agree, although the chart doesn't prove it directly. Other factors like homework could also matter.
Good point. We should mention that in our analysis.

grammar.title: Describing Trends: Nouns and Verbs
grammar.ar: يمكن وصف التغيّرات في الرسوم البيانية بطريقتين: باستخدام صفة + اسم مثل There was a sharp rise، أو باستخدام فعل + ظرف مثل The number rose sharply. ونستخدم According to the chart لنسب المعلومة إلى مصدرها. أما This suggests that فنستخدمها لتقديم تفسير أو استنتاج دون أن نؤكده تأكيداً تاماً.
examples: There was a sharp rise in gaming hours between 2019 and 2022.
Reading time dropped slightly among students aged fifteen and sixteen.
This suggests that teenagers prefer digital entertainment to books.

words.ex: Our team has five minutes to pitch our idea to the school principal.
A school garden would benefit students by teaching them about healthy food.
We want a sustainable project that continues after we graduate.
The project has a small budget, so we'll need to find sponsors.
The teachers asked whether the plan was feasible within one term.
She addressed the parents' concerns about safety very clearly.

dialogue.t: Good morning, everyone. The idea behind this project is to start a book exchange corner in our school library.
This would benefit students by giving them free access to books and encouraging them to read more.
Thank you. I have a question: how would you make sure the books come back?
That's a great question — what I mean is that it's an exchange, not a loan. You take a book only if you bring one.
I see. And who would organise it every week?
We already have six student volunteers, and the librarian has agreed to supervise.
It sounds feasible. Would you need any budget?
Very little — just some shelves and labels. We'd raise the money with a bake sale.

grammar.title: Using 'would' for Proposals
grammar.ar: عند تقديم فكرة مشروع لم يُنفَّذ بعد، نستخدم would + الفعل في صيغته الأساسية لأننا نتحدث عن نتائج متوقعة أو افتراضية. وفي عبارة This would benefit ... by ... يأتي بعد by فعل بصيغة ing لشرح الطريقة. ونستخدم That's a great question — what I mean is ... للرد على الأسئلة بلباقة وتوضيح ما قصدناه.
examples: This would benefit younger students by giving them older mentors to talk to.
The recycling bins would reduce plastic waste in the cafeteria.
That's a great question — what I mean is that volunteers would only work one hour a week.

words.ex: We can only speculate about why they are all standing on the roof of the car.
Her facial expression shows that she's more surprised than scared.
Judging by his body language, he's feeling quite relaxed.
The boy on the right looks puzzled, as if he doesn't understand what's going on.
In the background, you can see some people running towards the building.
Apparently, they've been waiting there for quite a long time.

dialogue.t: Look at this photo. They might be waiting for help because the water around the car is really deep.
Maybe, but it looks as if they're actually enjoying it. They're all laughing!
True. The man in the middle can't be scared. He's clearly making a joke about the whole thing.
What about the girl on the left? She looks a bit puzzled to me.
She might be a tourist because she's taking photos of everything around her.
And look at the sky in the background. It looks as if the rain has just stopped.
So they can't be in real danger anymore. They're clearly just waiting for the water to go down.
Exactly. I'd say they're making the best of a bad situation.

grammar.title: Present Deduction: might, can't, must & It looks as if
grammar.ar: نستخدم might أو could عندما نخمّن شيئًا ممكنًا لكننا غير متأكدين، وcan't عندما نكون متأكدين أن الشيء غير صحيح، وmust أو clearly عندما نكون شبه متأكدين أنه صحيح. يأتي بعد هذه الأفعال المصدر مثل be أو be + فعل ينتهي بـ ing. أما It looks as if فتتبعها جملة كاملة (فاعل + فعل) لوصف ما يبدو من الصورة. لاحظ أن عكس must في الاستنتاج هو can't وليس mustn't.
examples: They might be a family on holiday because they're carrying lots of suitcases.
It looks as if the woman has just received some good news.
He can't be a professional photographer. He's clearly using his phone camera.

words.ex: The disappearance of the crew is still unexplained after 150 years.
There's no real evidence that pirates attacked the ship.
One popular theory is that a sudden storm hit the area.
The whole crew seemed to vanish without leaving a single message.
That's the most plausible explanation I've heard so far.
Divers discovered the shipwreck near the coast of the Red Sea.

dialogue.t: Have you heard about the Mary Celeste? It was found floating in the Atlantic in 1872 with nobody on board.
Nobody at all? It must have been pirates, surely.
But nothing was stolen. The cargo and the crew's belongings were all still there.
Then maybe there was a storm. They could have got into the lifeboat instead of staying on the ship.
That's one theory. But there's no way they would have left a safe ship unless they thought it was about to sink.
Wasn't the cargo alcohol? Strong fumes could have made them think it was going to explode.
Exactly. That sounds the most plausible to me. They must have panicked and then got lost at sea.
It's a bit scary to think we'll probably never know for sure what happened.

grammar.title: Past Deduction: must have, could have, would have
grammar.ar: للتخمين حول أحداث وقعت في الماضي نستخدم: must have + التصريف الثالث للفعل عندما نكون شبه متأكدين، وcould have أو might have + التصريف الثالث عندما يكون الأمر محتملًا فقط، وcan't have + التصريف الثالث عندما نكون متأكدين أنه لم يحدث. وتُستخدم there's no way they would have ... unless ... لنقول إن شيئًا ما مستحيل إلا بشرط معيّن. انتبه: نقول must have gone وليس must have went.
examples: The ancient city must have been destroyed by a huge sandstorm.
They could have travelled by sea instead of crossing the desert.
There's no way they would have left their gold behind unless they were in serious danger.

words.ar: مُستدام / صديق للبيئة على المدى الطويل
words.ex: NEOM aims to be one of the most sustainable cities in the world.
Qiddiya is one of the giga-projects connected to Vision 2030.
By 2040, most of our electricity might come from renewable energy like solar power.
I'd love to ride in a driverless taxi through Riyadh.
AlUla has become a popular tourist destination for visitors from all over the world.
The country is investing billions in new roads, railways and other infrastructure.

dialogue.t: What do you think Saudi Arabia will be like in 2040?
By 2040, we'll probably have driverless taxis in every major city. The Riyadh Metro is already running, after all.
True. And it's likely that The Line in NEOM will have thousands of residents by then.
Maybe, but I doubt that it will be completely finished. It's such a huge project.
Fair point. What about tourism? I think the Red Sea resorts will be famous all over the world.
Definitely. It's likely that millions of tourists will visit AlUla and Qiddiya every year.
And it's unlikely that people will still drive petrol cars, don't you think?
I'm not so sure. I doubt that everyone will switch to electric cars that quickly, but renewable energy will probably power most homes.

grammar.title: Future Predictions with Degrees of Certainty
grammar.ar: عند التنبؤ بالمستقبل نُظهر مدى تأكدنا باستخدام تعبيرات مختلفة. نضع probably بعد will (we'll probably have) لكن قبل won't (we probably won't). ونستخدم It's likely / unlikely that + جملة كاملة للحديث عن احتمال مرتفع أو منخفض، وI doubt that ... will ... عندما لا نصدّق أن شيئًا سيحدث. وتعني By 2040 «بحلول عام 2040»، أي قبل ذلك التاريخ أو عنده.
examples: By 2040, we'll probably have flying taxis between Riyadh and Jeddah.
I doubt that people will stop visiting traditional markets completely.
It's unlikely that the desert will disappear, but it's likely that we'll see more green spaces in our cities.

words.ex: If I were the principal, I'd let students have a longer break.
I think the curriculum should include more practical skills like coding.
Our timetable is so packed that we barely have time to breathe.
Extracurricular activities like debate clubs help students build confidence.
Students often complain that their homework workload is too heavy.
Even small changes to the school day could make a big difference.

dialogue.t: If you were the principal for a day, what would you change?
The first thing I'd do is start school an hour later. Most of us are half asleep in the first lesson.
Ha, I'd vote for that! If I were the minister of education, I would reduce the homework workload.
Interesting. But suppose students could choose all their own subjects. What would happen?
I think they'd be more motivated, although some might just pick the easiest ones.
Good point. If I were in charge, I'd also add more extracurricular activities, like robotics and debate clubs.
And I'd make sure every school had a proper sports hall. That would really make a difference.
Sounds like we'd make a great team. Maybe we should send our ideas to the principal!

grammar.title: Second Conditional & Suppose
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثانية للحديث عن مواقف خيالية أو غير مرجّحة في الحاضر أو المستقبل: If + الماضي البسيط، ثم would + المصدر. في الأسلوب الرسمي والصحيح نقول If I were مع جميع الضمائر بدلًا من was. ويمكن استخدام Suppose + الماضي البسيط لطرح فكرة خيالية، ثم نسأل what would happen? لاحظ أن الفعل بعد If يكون في الماضي رغم أن المعنى عن الحاضر.
examples: If I were the minister of education, I would make coding a compulsory subject.
The first thing I'd do is give every student a tablet.
Suppose students could design their own timetable, what would happen?

words.ex: I really regret not taking part in the school trip last year.
When I look back on that day, I realise I overreacted.
Things turned out much better than I expected.
I missed the chance to meet my favourite author because I arrived late.

words.ar: بعد فوات الأوان / عند النظر إلى ما حدث
words.ex: In hindsight, choosing that subject was a great decision.
I forgot my passport once, and I definitely learned my lesson.

dialogue.t: Is there any decision you'd make differently if you could go back?
Yes. Last year I quit the football team because I thought it took up too much time. I wish I hadn't done that.
Really? What happened?
Well, they won the regional championship. If I had stayed, I would have played in the final.
That's tough. For me, it was the science fair. Looking back, I should have started my project much earlier.
Did it turn out badly?
Not terribly, but if I had planned better, I would have had time to test it properly. I definitely learned my lesson.
Same here. Next time I'll think twice before giving up on something.

grammar.title: Third Conditional, wish + Past Perfect & should have
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثالثة للحديث عن ماضٍ لم يحدث ونتائجه الخيالية: If + الماضي التام (had + التصريف الثالث)، ثم would have + التصريف الثالث. ونعبّر عن الندم على شيء فعلناه أو لم نفعله في الماضي بـ I wish + الماضي التام. أما should have + التصريف الثالث فتعني «كان يجب أن...» ولكننا لم نفعل. انتبه: لا نستخدم would بعد If في الجزء الأول من الجملة.
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam easily.
I wish I hadn't said those things to my best friend.
Looking back, I should have listened to my parents' advice.

words.ex: Choosing between two friends' parties was a real dilemma for me.
If I found a phone in the mall, I'd hand it in to security.
I'd feel guilty if I kept money that wasn't mine.
I promised to help him, so I don't want to let him down.
It's hard to turn down an invitation from a close friend.
The trip sounds fun. On the other hand, I have an important exam the next day.

dialogue.t: Okay, here's a dilemma. You find a wallet with 500 riyals in it, but there's no ID card. What would you do?
In that situation, I'd probably hand it in to the police, as long as the station wasn't too far away.
Really? Some people would just keep it.
Unless I knew for sure that nobody would claim it, I wouldn't keep a single riyal. I'd feel too guilty.
Fair enough. What about this one? Two friends invite you to their events on the same evening.
It depends on whether one of them is a special occasion, like a graduation.
Let's say one is a birthday and the other is a graduation party.
Then I'd go to the graduation, as long as I could explain it to my other friend. I wouldn't want to let anyone down without telling them.

grammar.title: Conditions with as long as, unless & it depends on whether
grammar.ar: نستخدم as long as بمعنى «بشرط أن»، وunless بمعنى «إلا إذا» أي if not، لذلك لا نضع بعدها فعلًا منفيًا (نقول unless I knew وليس unless I didn't know). وتُستخدم It depends on whether ... للقول إن القرار يعتمد على أمر معيّن قد يكون صحيحًا أو لا. وعند الحديث عن مواقف خيالية نستخدم الماضي البسيط بعد هذه الروابط مع would في الجزء الآخر من الجملة.
examples: In that situation, I'd probably tell the teacher, as long as my friend didn't get into serious trouble.
Unless I had a really good reason, I wouldn't turn down my cousin's wedding invitation.
It depends on whether the owner's phone number is inside the wallet.
